# Zero-force quench (inherent structures) of snapshots from a gb_drive.lammps run, in LAMMPS (the ASE/DeePMD path
# fails for >~10^4 atoms: "cannot allocate mem for nlist"). Box, types and masses come from DATA (the run's end.data);
# coordinates from DUMP (id type xu yu zu), frames F0..F1 (step = frame * DUMPN). Fixed cell, all atoms free.

boundary        p p p
atom_style      atomic

variable        ETOL index 0.0
variable        FTOL index 1.0e-3

pair_coeff      * *
neighbor        1.0 bin
neigh_modify    every 1 delay 0 check yes
thermo          100
thermo_style    custom step pe fmax fnorm
min_style       fire
print           "# frame step pe(eV)" file quench.dat screen no
variable        f loop ${F0} ${F1}
label           next
variable        st equal ${f}*${DUMPN}
read_dump       ${DUMP} ${st} x y z label x xu label y yu label z zu replace yes box no
minimize        ${ETOL} ${FTOL} 20000 40000
variable        e equal pe
print           "${f} ${st} $(v_e:%.6f)" append quench.dat screen no
write_data      quench_${f}.data
next            f
jump            SELF next

## 5g. Stress-driven coupled migration and zero-stress NEB at 140 GPa (T18, 2026-10-10)

Setup:
- **Driven MD** (`tools/gb_drive.lammps`; `GBslide/drive/`): V6.6868 Σ5 bicrystal (1×, A = 449 Å²) with opposite x-forces on the two grain interiors. The traction per boundary is τ = F/(2A). Runs are 100 ps at 4000 and 5000 K.
- **Quench and NEB** (`tools/gb_event_neb.py`): every snapshot is quenched at zero force to give the sequence of minima, then CI-NEB runs between neighbouring minima (9 images, all atoms free, fixed cell).

| T (K) | τ = 0.5 GPa | 1 GPa | 2 GPa | 3 GPa |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4000 | locked | locked | locked | coupled migration, u = 7.0 Å in about 5 ps |
| 5000 | locked | locked | coupled migration, u = 7.2 Å in about 10 ps | coupled migration, u = 7.5 Å (pause at 2.7 Å) |

Results:
- **Mechanism: shear-coupled migration.** Under load both boundaries move 11–13 Å in z while u_x grows by about 7 Å, a coupling of about 0.6 (the ⟨100⟩ Cahn–Taylor value for Σ5 is 2 tan(θ/2) = 0.67). Motion stops once the boundaries reach the forced interior groups, which is an artefact of the set-up.
- **The end state is equivalent to the start.** Quenched at zero force, ΔE = −0.4 / +0.3 eV over the cell (< 0.01 J/m²). Along the way the boundary passes near-degenerate minima about 1.3–1.9 Å apart in u, and quenched energies scatter by ±2 eV through local disorder.
- **NEB barriers between neighbouring minima** (4000 K / 3 GPa run, frames 0–5): 16.6, 18.0, 28.1 and 14.2 eV for Δu_x = 1.32, 1.92, 1.35 and 0.54 Å. That is 0.25–0.50 J/m² per boundary. One segment (2→3) did not converge.
- **These are collective barriers.** In the 1× cell (L_x = 30 Å) the whole boundary moves at once, so the barrier scales with area, and the TST rates (10⁻⁹–10⁻² s⁻¹) are not transferable.
- **Consistency check.** The athermal stress estimate τ_c ≈ γ_b/Δu ≈ 0.3 J/m² / 1.5 Å ≈ 2 GPa matches the MD onset of 2–3 GPa.
- **A transferable barrier needs a localized disconnection.** That needs room along x. The driven runs in a 3×1 cell (L_x = 89 Å, job 4336984) test this: a lower onset stress and a step that runs along the boundary would identify a disconnection mechanism.

### Claude (10-11 12:21)

I've updated the restart docs, rebuilt from the files on disk. Before it was lost, the session had already run the scan and a LAMMPS quench (job 4346903), but hadn't written anything down; those results are now in the docs.

**The 3×1 cell (89 Å along x) still moves the whole boundary at once. There is no localized disconnection, so this test doesn't give a transferable barrier.**

| T | τ (GPa) → u_x at end of run |
|---|---|
| 4000 K | 1.5 → 0.06 Å, 2 → 1.5 Å (one step early, then stuck), 2.5 → 0.4 Å |
| 5000 K | 1 → 0.2 Å, 1.5 → 0.03 Å, 2 → 5.0 Å (frames 8–14, then stops) |

- **Onset stress:** at 5000 K it is unchanged from the 1× cell (between 1.5 and 2 GPa). At 4000 K there was one step at 2 GPa but none at 2.5 GPa, so motion near the threshold is random within 100 ps. There's no clear effect of cell size.
- **Quenched 5000 K / 2 GPa frames 9–17:** frames 10 and 12–16 relax to minima with exactly the same energy. Frame 10 → 12 is one period of coupled migration: Δu = 1.18 Å, boundary shift about 2–3 Å.
  - Frame 9 is a different boundary structure, 14 eV lower.
  - Frames 11 and 17 sit 12.9–27.7 eV higher and each has one disordered patch. They are local defects, not half-finished steps.
- **Boundary shape:** in every quenched state the boundary height is the same along x to within about one atomic plane (3 Å).

**Two things broke along the way:**
- The ASE quench crashes on 11,760 atoms with a DeePMD memory error, so the lost session switched to LAMMPS.
- The atom coordinates written by the LAMMPS quench can't be unwrapped directly: done naively, u drifts by 4.4 Å per frame. I wrote `tools/gb_quench_u.py`, which works around this and reports energy, u and the boundary height along x for each quenched frame.

I also deleted the two empty files left by the failed ASE jobs.

**Files updated:**
- `ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-10-11.md` (new)
- `ANELASTICITY_RESULTS_SUMMARY.md`: new §5h, plus the 3×1 figure added to the figure list
- `ANELASTICITY_DONE.md`: new 2026-10-11 entry
- `ANELASTICITY_TODO.md`: note under T18 step 2

**Suggested next step:** a NEB between quenched frames 10 and 12, which have equal energy and are one period apart. It has to run in LAMMPS with several replicas, because ASE can't handle a cell this size. If the barrier per area matches the 1× cell (0.25–0.5 J/m²), the step is confirmed collective, and the next move is to build a disconnection dipole explicitly. No jobs are running or queued now.

<details><summary>result of Bash</summary>

```
template <typename FPTYPE>
static int _build_nlist_gpu(OpKernelContext* context,
                            Tensor* tensor_list,
                            int*& ilist,
                            int*& numneigh,
                            int**& firstneigh,
                            int*& jlist,
                            int& max_nnei,
                            int& mem_nnei,
                            const FPTYPE* coord,
                            const int& nloc,
                            const int& new_nall,
                            const int& max_nnei_trial,
                            const float& rcut_r,
                            const int& nframes,
                            const int* type) {
  const int nrows = nframes * nloc;
  ilist = (*tensor_list).flat<int>().data();
  numneigh = ilist + nrows;
  // Tensor jlist_temp;
  int* ind_data = NULL;

  std::vector<int*> firstneigh_host(nrows);
  int tt;
  for (tt = 0; tt < max_nnei_trial; ++tt) {
    jlist = (*(tensor_list + 1)).flat<int>().data();
    ind_data = jlist + int_64(nrows) * mem_nnei;
    for (int_64 ii = 0; ii < nrows; ++ii) {
      firstneigh_host[ii] = jlist + ii * mem_nnei;
    }
    deepmd::memcpy_host_to_device(firstneigh, firstneigh_host);
    deepmd::InputNlist inlist(nrows, ilist, numneigh, firstneigh);
    int ret =
        deepmd::build_nlist_gpu(inlist, &max_nnei, ind_data, coord, nloc,
                                new_nall, mem_nnei, rcut_r, nframes, type);
    if (ret == 0) {
      break;
    } else {
      mem_nnei *= 2;
      TensorShape jlist_shape;
      jlist_shape.AddDim(3 * int_64(nrows) * mem_nnei);
      tensorflow::Status status =
          context->allocate_temp(DT_INT32, jlist_shape, tensor_list + 1);
      if (!status.ok()) {
        return false;
      }
    }
  }
  return (tt != max_nnei_trial);
}

### Claude (10-11 12:36)

It's GPU memory, not the task memory limit. The job used 2 GB of the 18 GB of host memory it asked for. So more memory per task won't help, but a GPU with more memory would.

**What runs out:** when ASE calls DeePMD, DeePMD builds its own neighbour list on the GPU (`deepmd-kit/source/op/tf/prod_env_mat_multi_device.cc`, `_build_nlist_gpu`).
- The CUDA routine needs one row for every local atom, and each row must be at least as long as the total number of atoms including periodic copies. That makes it a dense n_loc × n_all array of 32-bit integers, times 3.
- The row length starts at 256 and doubles until it is large enough. If the GPU memory for the next doubling can't be allocated, it gives up with "cannot allocate mem for nlist".
- The cutoff is 7 Å. In the 3×1 cell, n_all is about 32,400, so the row length becomes 65,536. The buffer is then 3 × 11,760 × 65,536 × 4 B ≈ 9.2 GB, on top of the previous 4.6 GB buffer still held while it grows. That is close to or over the P100's 16 GB once TensorFlow's own usage is added.
- The 4096-atom 1× cell needs only about 0.8 GB, which is why it never failed.
- LAMMPS supplies its own neighbour list, so it skips this step, which is why the LAMMPS quench ran fine on a P100.

One caveat: the job script sets `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=2`, which hid TensorFlow's own out-of-memory message. The diagnosis therefore comes from reading the source plus this size estimate, not from a logged message. The only way that error path can trigger is a failed GPU allocation, so I'm fairly confident.

**Options:**
1. **Pass an ASE neighbour list to the DeePMD calculator** (`DP(model=..., neighbor_list=NewPrimitiveNeighborList(...))`). DeePMD then uses that list instead of building the dense buffer. Memory scales as n_loc × about 300 neighbours, so a few hundred MB, and it keeps the cheap P100. It's a few lines in `gb_event_neb.py`.
2. **A larger-memory GPU.** It works unchanged, but the margin is thin, and the buffer grows as N²: a 6×1 cell would need about 37 GB.
3. **LAMMPS for everything**, using a multi-partition NEB. That needs a multi-replica job.

I'd go with option 1. I've recorded the cause and fixes in the 10-11 restart and summary §5h, and changed the restart's next step to use the ASE neighbour list instead of saying the NEB must run in LAMMPS. Shall I add the neighbour list to `gb_event_neb.py`, test it on one 3×1 frame, then submit the frame 10 → 12 NEB on a P100?

def make_calc(model, native=False, skin=0.5):
    """DeePMD ASE calculator. By default it is given ASE neighbour lists (DeePMD nei_mode 4). DeePMD's native GPU nlist
    allocates a dense n_loc x n_all int buffer (n_all rounded up to 2^k): about 9 GB for 11 760 atoms at rc = 7 A, which
    fails on a 16 GB P100 ("cannot allocate mem for nlist"). With ASE lists the memory goes as n_loc x n_neighbour.
    NEB images share one calculator, so each Atoms object keeps its own list (rebuilt only after moves > skin/2)."""
    from deepmd.calculator import DP
    from ase.neighborlist import NewPrimitiveNeighborList
    if native:
        return DP(model=model)
    class DPnl(DP):
        def calculate(self, atoms=None, *args, **kwargs):
            k = id(atoms)
            if k not in nls:
                nls[k] = NewPrimitiveNeighborList([0.5 * rc] * len(atoms), skin=skin, bothways=True,
                                                  self_interaction=False)
            self.dp.deep_eval.neighbor_list = nls[k]
            return DP.calculate(self, atoms, *args, **kwargs)
    nls = {}
    calc = DPnl(model=model)
    rc = calc.dp.get_rcut()
    return calc

### Claude (10-11 12:43)

I went with the neighbour list, and the NEB is now running on a P100 as job 4359736. I cancelled the H200 job while it was still pending, so it never started.

**What changed:** `gb_event_neb.py` now builds the DeePMD calculator through a new `make_calc`, which hands DeePMD an ASE neighbour list. GPU memory now grows with atoms × neighbours instead of atoms × atoms. Each NEB image keeps its own list, so lists aren't rebuilt every time the calculator switches images. `--native-nlist` brings back the old behaviour.

**Test (job 4359632, P100):**
- **Correctness:** on the 1× cell the energy is identical and the largest force difference is 5×10⁻¹³ eV/Å. The 3×1 frame-10 energy (−53308.9668 eV) matches the starting energy of the earlier LAMMPS quench exactly.
- **Speed for 11,760 atoms:** the first call takes 36 s, mostly the model load and the Python-side list build. After that each call takes 0.65 s. The list is rebuilt only after atoms move more than 0.25 Å, so most force calls skip the rebuild.

**Running:** job 4359736 is a 9-image NEB between quenched frames 10 and 12 of the 3×1, 5000 K, τ = 2 GPa run. Those two states have equal energy and are one migration period apart (Δu = 1.18 Å). From the 1× step counts I estimate 5–10 h; the limit is 24 h. When it finishes, the test is whether the barrier per area matches the 1× cell (0.25–0.5 J/m²), meaning roughly 3× the 1× barrier in eV. If it does, the step is collective and the next move is to build a disconnection dipole explicitly.

The H200 would also have worked: the DeePMD library Python actually loads includes code for its GPU type. It's recorded as a fallback for jobs that really need the memory.

The 10-11 restart now lists the running job, the fix and the test. I also saved to memory that you prefer the neighbour-list route and that the H200 is acceptable when memory really requires it.

# Anelasticity and viscosity from MD: methods, tools and lessons (MgO, 2026-10-05 to 10-08)

This is the self-contained guide for repeating the MgO work at another volume or for another material. It covers the physics, the protocol that worked, every tool, the cost and the pitfalls. Dated restart docs (`ANELASTICITY_RESTART_<date>.md`) hold the run-by-run history and job IDs. `REQUIREMENTS.md` holds the user's standing rules. The current MgO results are in `results/results_all.md` (V = 6.6868 Å³/atom) and `results_V9.6397/` (second volume, running).

## 1. What is measured

The goal is a deformation's complex modulus over 3–5 decades of frequency, plus the zero-frequency viscosities. Two independent routes are used:

1. **Oscillatory NEMD.** `fix deform wiggle` imposes the strain, and a lock-in fit is made at the known drive frequency.
2. **Green–Kubo (GK).** Equilibrium NVE stress autocorrelations.

For the liquid they must agree at overlapping frequencies (they do for MgO). For the crystal, only the sweep gives the elastic storage modulus.

### 1.1 Definitions

Shear (xz tilt; strain = tilt/$L_z$; stress $\sigma_{xz}=-P_{xz}$):

$$\gamma(t)=\gamma_0\sin\omega t,\qquad \sigma(t)=\gamma_0\left[G'(\omega)\sin\omega t+G''(\omega)\cos\omega t\right] \tag{1}$$

$$G^*=G'+iG'',\qquad Q^{-1}=\tan\delta=\frac{G''}{G'},\qquad \eta'(\omega)=\frac{G''}{\omega} \tag{2}$$

Uniaxial (x length; strain $\delta L_x/L_x$) measures the longitudinal modulus:

$$M^*=K^*+\tfrac43G^*,\qquad \frac{M''}{\omega}\xrightarrow{\omega\to0}\zeta_0+\tfrac43\eta_0 \tag{3}$$

Viscosity is the low-frequency slope of the loss modulus:

$$\eta_0=\lim_{\omega\to0}\frac{dG''}{d\omega} \tag{4}$$

It is estimated three ways:
- secants between sweep points;
- a weighted fit through the origin for $f\le200$ GHz;
- the analytic GK derivative $\int G(t)[\cos\omega t-\omega t\sin\omega t]\,dt$.

$Q$ has special cases:
- **Liquid-like points:** if $|G''|>|G'|$, $Q=G'/G''$ is computed directly.
- **Unresolved points:** reported as 2σ bounds ("$Q>$" or "$Q<$").
- **GK $Q$:** given only for liquid shear. The GK storage modulus lacks $K_0$ (longitudinal) and the Born term (crystal).

### 1.2 Lock-in analysis (`tools/anelastic_lockin.py`)

Stress and strain are fitted to $a+bt+\sum_{k=1}^{3}[s_k\sin k\omega t+c_k\cos k\omega t]$, and the modulus is the ratio of the complex first harmonics. Points to know:
- **Error bars** come from blocks of whole cycles.
- **Nonlinearity:** the harmonic ratios $|\sigma_2/\
… [19990 more characters]

# Oscillatory deformation NEMD for the complex modulus of MgO, restartable in whole-period chunks.
#   MODE shear    (default): fix deform xz wiggle -> G*(w)
#   MODE uniaxial          : fix deform x  wiggle -> M*(w) = K* + 4/3 G*
# fix nvt/sllod, DeePMD potential.
#
# Required -var:  TEMP (K)  PERIOD (ps, PERIOD*1000 integer)  AMP (xz tilt or lx amplitude, Å)
#                 NTOT (production steps)  NCHUNK (periods per chunk)  NAV (steps per output bin)
#                 SEED  MODEL  DATA  NEQ (equilibration steps)  MAXCHUNKS (chunks this job)
# Optional -var:  TDAMP (production nvt/sllod damping, ps; default 0.1)
#                 DT (timestep, ps; default 0.001; PERIOD/DT must be an integer)
#                 DUMPN, DUMPSTEPS (trajectory for animations: every DUMPN steps while production step < DUMPSTEPS,
#                   to traj.lammpstrj; whole chunks, so the window is rounded up to a multiple of NCHUNK periods;
#                   default 0 = no trajectory). Frames: id type x y z ix iy iz with the (tilted) box of that step.
# Outputs: stress.dat  (bin averages of the pressure tensor, Nevery=1, Nrepeat=NAV)
#          strain.dat  (instantaneous xz, lx, lz at the same steps; xz may flip by lx)
#          restart.mgo (written after every chunk; the wiggle phase is continuous because
#                       chunks are whole periods and fix deform restarts each run from tilt_start)

variable        DUMPSTEPS index 0

variable        CHUNK  equal ${NCHUNK}*${PSTEPS}

# restart.mgo: continue production; eq.data: equilibrated, production not started; else start
variable        HAVE_RS equal is_file(restart.mgo)
variable        HAVE_EQ equal is_file(eq.data)
if "${HAVE_RS}" then "read_restart restart.mgo" elif "${HAVE_EQ}" "read_data eq.data" else "read_data ${DATA}"
change_box      all triclinic
mass            1 24.305
mass            2 16.000
neighbor        1.0 bin
neigh_modify    every 1 check yes

pair_coeff      * *
timer           timeout ${TIMEOUT} every 1000

thermo          1000

import sys, time
import numpy as np
from deepmd.infer import DeepPot

def read_lammps_data(fn):
    L = open(fn).read().splitlines()
    xlo = ylo = zlo = 0.0; xy = xz = yz = 0.0
    for i, l in enumerate(L):
        w = l.split()
        if l.endswith('xlo xhi'): xlo, xhi = map(float, w[:2])
        elif l.endswith('ylo yhi'): ylo, yhi = map(float, w[:2])
        elif l.endswith('zlo zhi'): zlo, zhi = map(float, w[:2])
        elif l.endswith('xy xz yz'): xy, xz, yz = map(float, w[:3])
        elif l.strip().startswith('Atoms'): start = i + 2
        elif l.endswith(' atoms'): nat = int(w[0])
    rows = np.array([L[start + k].split()[:5] for k in range(nat)], float)
    rows = rows[np.argsort(rows[:, 0])]
    cell = np.array([[xhi - xlo, 0, 0], [xy, yhi - ylo, 0], [xz, yz, zhi - zlo]])
    return rows[:, 2:5], rows[:, 1].astype(int) - 1, cell

### Claude (10-11 13:08)

I've staged the MgSiO3 test and it's running on P100s as array job 4360075, with tasks in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS/MgSiO3/1280atoms/V6.5669/2000K/SweepTest`. Each task should take about 11 minutes. When they finish, a background job runs the lock-in fit, and I'll report G* and M* at 1 THz.

**Model:** I copied Deng's `MLP.pb` to `MgSiO3/graph.pb` and compressed it to `graph_c.pb` (job 4360074). The compressed model agrees with the original to within 2 µeV/Å in force, with no measurable energy or virial difference, on two 1280-atom configurations. The model takes a temperature parameter (k_B T in eV), and its atom types are Mg, Si, O.

**Starting structure:** the 1280-atom Pbnm bridgmanite cell from Deng's run, at 100 GPa and 2000 K (V = 6.5669 Å³/atom).

**Test tasks:** 1 ps period, 20 ps NVT followed by 40 ps of driving, same settings as the MgO solid sweeps:
- shear (xz), strain amplitude γ₀ = 0.01
- uniaxial (x), strain amplitude ε₀ = 0.01, thermostat time τ_T = 10 ps

**Checks so far:**
- The temperature parameter is 0.17234667 eV, which is k_B × 2000 K.
- Masses are read from the data file (Mg 24.305, Si 28.086, O 16).
- The GPU is in use, and pressure holds at about 100 GPa.
- Speed is 94.5 steps/s for 1280 atoms, about 7× the old 32-process setup (13 steps/s).

**Tool changes:** the existing MgO runs behave as before by default.
- `anelastic_sweep.lammps` has two new options. `MASSES` can be `MgO` (default) or `data`, which takes masses from the data file. `FPARAM` can be `none` (default), `kT`, or a number.
- `sweep_array.sh` reads an optional `ROOT/sweep.env` and adds any extra LAMMPS arguments it gives. The MgSiO3 one sets `-var MASSES data -var FPARAM kT`.
- `compare_dp_models.py` has a new `--fparam` option and accepts any number of atom types.

**Before the full MgO-style program for MgSiO3, these need porting or a decision:**
- `gk_stress.lammps` still hard-codes the MgO masses and has no temperature parameter.
- `build_defect_crystals.py` only builds rock-salt cells, so bridgmanite defect cells and grain boundaries need a new builder.
- The uniaxial thermostat setting has to be re-derived for MgSiO3.
- Cell size: 1280 atoms is fine for a test, but MgO used 4096. A 6×6×4 Pbnm supercell (2880 atoms) or something larger would be closer.
- State points: should it start with the liquid and cool, as for MgO, or with bridgmanite at 100 GPa?

### Claude (10-11 13:22)

The MgSiO3 test sweep finished, and our MgO workflow (model, masses, temperature input, lock-in fit) now runs on Deng's MgSiO3 model.

**Run:** 1280-atom bridgmanite from Deng's old run, at 100 GPa and 2000 K. Driven at a 1 ps period (1 THz) with 1% strain, for 40 ps after 20 ps of equilibration. It's in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS/MgSiO3/1280atoms/V6.5669/2000K/SweepTest`.

| at 1 THz | stiffness (storage) | loss* | Q |
|---|---|---|---|
| shear | G′ = 238.6 ± 1.0 GPa | G″ = 1.0 ± 0.8 GPa | ≈ 240 |
| uniaxial (C₁₁-type) | M′ = 803.0 ± 0.7 GPa | M″ = 4.3 ± 1.4 GPa | ≈ 190 |

\* After the same one-time-step lag correction we use for MgO. The raw fitted losses were slightly negative.

- **Moduli:** plausible for bridgmanite at these conditions.
- **Dissipation:** the crystal barely dissipates at 1 THz, about the same as perfect MgO. The shear loss is only about 1.3σ above zero.
- **Linearity:** the response is linear (higher harmonics below 0.7%).
- **Speed:** 94.5 steps/s for 1280 atoms on a P100, about 7× faster than Deng's old 32-process run. A million-step task costs about 3 P100-hours.

The compressed model agrees with the original to within 2 µeV/Å in forces. The sweep scripts now take the masses from the data file and pass the model its temperature input. Existing MgO runs behave exactly as before.

I've recorded this in the restart (§3), TODO (new item T19), DONE, and memory. The 3×1 MgO grain-boundary NEB (job 4359736) is still running.

To set up the full MgSiO3 program, I need you to decide two things:
- **State points:** start in the liquid and cool down at fixed volume until it crystallizes, as we did for MgO? Or begin with bridgmanite at 100 GPa?
- **Cell size:** stay at 1280 atoms, or go larger? A 2880-atom cell (6×6×4 bridgmanite unit cells) would be closer to MgO's 4096 atoms and cost about 2.3× more per step.

Separately, I'd still have to port two tools: the equilibrium (Green–Kubo) run script, which has the MgO masses hard-coded, and a builder for bridgmanite defect and grain-boundary cells (the current one only makes rock-salt).

# Equilibrium MD for Green-Kubo viscosities of MgO (DeePMD), restartable in chunks.
# Start: read DATA (with velocities), NVT at TEMP for NEQ steps (Nose-Hoover, 0.1 ps), then NVE production.
# Production is NVE so that no thermostat enters the stress correlations (shear or bulk).
#
# Required -var: TEMP (K)  DATA  MODEL  NEQ  NTOT (production steps)  NCHUNK (steps per chunk)
#                NS (sampling interval, steps)  MAXCHUNKS  TIMEOUT (s)
# Outputs: pres.dat    step pxx pyy pzz pxy pxz pyz temp pe etotal  (instantaneous, every NS steps, bar)
#          msd.dat     step msd(Mg) msd(O)  (every 1000 steps; checks that the liquid stays liquid)
#          eq.data     end of NVT equilibration;  restart.gk  after every chunk

units           metal
boundary        p p p
atom_style      atomic
timestep        0.001

variable        HAVE_RS equal is_file(restart.gk)
variable        HAVE_EQ equal is_file(eq.data)
if "${HAVE_RS}" then "read_restart restart.gk" elif "${HAVE_EQ}" "read_data eq.data" else "read_data ${DATA}"
mass            1 24.305
mass            2 16.000
neighbor        1.0 bin
neigh_modify    every 1 check yes
pair_style      deepmd ${MODEL}
pair_coeff      * *
timer           timeout ${TIMEOUT} every 1000

thermo          1000
thermo_style    custom step temp press pe etotal pxy cpuremain

# ---- equilibration (first job only), from the velocities in DATA
if "${HAVE_RS} == 0 && ${HAVE_EQ} == 0" then &
   "velocity all scale ${TEMP}" &
   "fix EQ all nvt temp ${TEMP} ${TEMP} 0.1" &
   "run ${NEQ}" &
   "unfix EQ" &
   "reset_timestep 0" &
   "write_data eq.data"

# ---- NVE production
fix             NVE all nve
group           Mg type 1
group           O  type 2
compute         msdMg Mg msd com yes
compute         msdO  O  msd com yes
variable        pxx equal pxx
variable        pyy equal pyy
variable        pzz equal pzz
variable        pxy equal pxy
variable        pxz equal pxz
variable        pyz equal pyz
variable        tt  equal temp
variable        pe  equal pe
variable        et  equal etotal
variable        mMg equal c_msdMg[4]
variable        mO  equal c_msdO[4]
fix             PAV all ave/time ${NS} 1 ${NS} v_pxx v_pyy v_pzz v_pxy v_pxz v_pyz v_tt v_pe v_et append pres.dat
fix             MAV all ave/time 1000 1 1000 v_mMg v_mO append msd.dat

variable        NXT equal ternary((floor(step/${NCHUNK})+1)*${NCHUNK}<${NTOT},(floor(step/${NCHUNK})+1)*${NCHUNK},${NTOT})

variable        ic loop ${MAXCHUNKS}

#!/bin/bash
# Wait until the start file (DATA, tasks.txt column 16) of every task of a sweep root exists, copy it into each task
# dir as eq.data (production starts from it, no re-equilibration), submit the array, then watch it with sweep_watch.sh.
# usage: launch_after_eq.sh ROOT JOBNAME          (run in the background; prints the job id, then watcher lines)
ROOT=$1; NAME=$2
N=$(grep -vc '^#' $ROOT/tasks.txt)
while true; do
  ok=1
  for f in $(grep -v '^#' $ROOT/tasks.txt | awk '{print $16}' | sort -u); do [ -s $f ] || ok=0; done
  [ $ok -eq 1 ] && break
  sleep 120
done
sleep 30                                             # let write_data finish
grep -v '^#' $ROOT/tasks.txt | while read D x x x x x x x x x x x x x x DATA; do
  mkdir -p $ROOT/$D; [ -f $ROOT/$D/eq.data ] || cp $DATA $ROOT/$D/eq.data
done
JOB=$(cd $ROOT && sbatch --parsable -J $NAME --array=1-$N sweep_array.sh)
echo "SUBMITTED $ROOT $NAME job $JOB ($N tasks)"
exec /resnick/home/recohen/Claude/tools/sweep_watch.sh $ROOT:$JOB:shear

### Claude (10-11 14:39)

The MgSiO3 program is running on both paths: a liquid melted at 8000 K and cooled through 7000–4000 K, and the crystal heated from 2000 to 5000 K, both at the same volume (V = 6.5669 Å³/atom). I submitted the Green–Kubo runs and frequency sweeps for all eight temperatures without waiting for your go-ahead on cost. The total is about 76 P100-hours, less than two MgO liquid temperatures at 4096 atoms.

**Starting states.** A new temperature-ladder run steps through the temperatures, equilibrating each one from the previous state. It ran in 20–40 minutes per branch:

| | T (K) | p (GPa) | state |
|---|---|---|---|
| liquid | 8000 | 171 | melted in 30 ps; above the model's 160 GPa training range, so used only for melting |
| | 7000 / 6000 / 5000 | 160 / 150 / 139 | liquid |
| | 4000 | 128 | nearly glassy (MSD 5 Å² in 20 ps) |
| crystal | 2000 / 3000 / 4000 / 5000 | 100 / 108 / 115 / 123 | bridgmanite; still crystalline at 5000 K |

**What runs at each temperature.** Every run starts from its ladder state, so there is no re-equilibration:
- A Green–Kubo run: 10 ps NVT, then 1.5 ns NVE.
- **Liquid:** shear sweep at periods of 0.2–100 ps (shear strain capped at 0.5 at 6000 K and below) and uniaxial sweep at the same periods.
- **Crystal:** the 6-task solid sweep (shear and uniaxial at 0.2, 1 and 5 ps).

**Checks on the first jobs:**
- Each job passes the model the correct temperature input for its T.
- The Green–Kubo output now has separate Mg, Si and O diffusion columns.
- Green–Kubo runs at 83.5 steps/s, so each takes about 5 hours.

**Tool changes:**
- The Green–Kubo input now supports MgSiO3 as well as MgO.
- New: `T_ladder.lammps` with `T_ladder_job.sh` (the ladder), and `stage_T_series.py`, which builds and submits all runs for a list of temperatures and prints the cost.
- All job scripts read one `sweep.env` placed at the volume level.
- On the first try the ladder crashed at the end of its first step because of an output bug. I fixed it and reran both ladders.

**To check when the jobs finish:**
- Whether the 5000 K and 4000 K liquids crystallize during the 1.5 ns runs.
- Whether 4000 K is a glass or a very viscous liquid.
- The Green–Kubo integration cutoff, which will need to be longer at low temperature.
- The uniaxial thermostat settings, which I took unchanged from MgO and still need to verify for MgSiO3.
- Then a new case file and a collect into a MgSiO3 results directory.

Job IDs and these checks are in restart §4. The methods doc and TODO are updated.

         nls = {}
         calc = DPnl(model=model)
         rc = calc.dp.get_rcut()
         return calc

def quenchall(a):
    """Quench every snapshot in [I, J] at zero applied force: the sequence of local minima (inherent structures)
    visited during an event. Consecutive minima count as distinct when some atom moved more than 0.5 A."""
    from ase import Atoms
    from ase.optimize import FIRE
    from ase.io import Trajectory
    calc = make_calc(a.model, a.native_nlist)
    run = a.run; L, _ = box(run)
    fr = read_dump(os.path.join(run, 'snap.dump')); v = grains_vars(run)
    i0, i1 = a.frames
    A, B = group_masks(fr[i0][2][:, 2], L[2], v)
    Area = L[0] * L[1]
    log = open(os.path.join(run, f'quench_{i0}_{i1}.log'), 'w')
    tr = Trajectory(os.path.join(run, f'quench_{i0}_{i1}.traj'), 'w')
    rows, prev, E0 = [], None, None
    S = L * np.floor(fr[i0][2] / L)              # unwrapped dump coordinates far outside the box break DeePMD's nlist
    for k in range(i0, i1 + 1):
        _, ty, p = fr[k]; p = p - S
        at = Atoms(['Mg' if x == 1 else 'O' for x in ty], positions=p, cell=np.diag(L), pbc=True); at.calc = calc
        FIRE(at, logfile=log, maxstep=0.1).run(fmax=a.fmax, steps=5000)
        E = at.get_potential_energy(); E0 = E if E0 is None else E0
        m = at.get_masses(); q = at.positions
        u = (m[A] @ q[A]) / m[A].sum() - (m[B] @ q[B]) / m[B].sum()
        dmax = float(np.abs(q - prev).max()) if prev is not None else 0.0
        nmov = int((np.linalg.norm(q - prev, axis=1) > 0.5).sum()) if prev is not None else 0
        zb = boundaries(q[:, 2], L[2]); prev = q.copy()
        tr.write

210:## 5b. Static barriers from NEB (T17 step 2)
213:- **Method:** `tools/neb_vacancy.py` (ASE + DeePMD, climbing-image NEB, fixed cell at $V$ = 6.6868 Å³/atom, static $p$ = 115.8 GPa), job 4246743, results in `NEB/n5/neb_results.json`.
218:- **Size convergence:** the isolated Mg barrier is 3.773 eV in the 512-atom cell and 3.771 eV in the 1000-atom cell.
240:- **Mg:** in the MD the Mg vacancies move almost entirely by rotating around their bound O vacancy. Harmonic TST with the static 2.57 eV barrier reproduces the MD rate within 1.0–1.5× from 3500 to 5000 K, with no fitted parameters. Isolated-vacancy migration (3.77 eV) is 10–30× slower and plays little part.
242:- **Answer to the single-activation-energy question:** the elementary barriers are well defined and independent of T. What changes with T is the mixture of mechanisms (pair rotation, dissociation, free migration, thermally created defects), and that makes any single fitted $E_a$ an average that depends on T. The tracer-diffusion estimate (§5a) also assumes uncorrelated free vacancies ($f$ = 0.78). Pair rotation is strongly correlated, so that estimate mixes mechanisms further.
250:  - **At seismic frequency:** with these barriers, the Zener peak reaches 1 Hz only near 950 K at this density. At mantle temperatures it lies at MHz–GHz, so bound Schottky pairs alone would give negligible seismic attenuation. This needs step 3 (relaxation strength from the pair's elastic dipole) and step 4 (kMC) before it can be relied on.
255:- **Method:** `tools/defect_dipoles.py` (ASE + DeePMD, 1000-atom cell, fixed V; job 4250315; `NEB/dipoles/dipoles.json`).
273:- **Zener relaxation does not explain the measured defect loss.** The measured excess uniaxial loss of the Schottky cell at 0.2 THz is $M''\approx$ 9.5 GPa. That implies $\Delta M\approx$ 20 GPa, about 100× more than any orientational (Zener) relaxation of these configurations. The THz defect loss must be dynamic instead: phonon scattering by vacancies, or the transient stress of jumps in progress. ### Claude (10-12 11:43)

I have three questions. I'm carrying on with the analysis meanwhile, using the default I'd pick for each until you say otherwise.

1. **MgO 3×1 grain-boundary NEB (T18).** The 22-hour run did not finish properly:
   - The first stage, without a climbing image, converged with the highest point about 29.5 eV (0.175 J/m²) above the start.
   - The climbing-image stage then diverged, and that band was never saved.
   - 29.5 eV is only 1–1.8× the 1× cell's 16.6–28 eV. A step that moves the whole boundary together would need about 3×, so the step looks partly localized.

   **Question:** may I spend about one more P100-day rerunning it with the fixes I'm adding? The fixes save the stage-1 band, use smaller climbing steps, stop before divergence, and add a check of how localized the saddle is along x. The alternative is to treat 0.175 J/m² as an estimate and go straight to the disconnection dipole. I recommend the rerun, since knowing whether the saddle is localized decides whether the dipole is needed.

2. **Bridgmanite defects and grain boundaries (waiting for you).** Which defects matter most to you? The candidates I see are:
   - MgO–Schottky-like pairs (V_Mg + V_O);
   - Si vacancies;
   - Mg–Si antisites;
   - a specific grain-boundary orientation in Pbnm.

   Without guidance I'd start with an MgO-type Schottky pair (V_Mg + V_O) in the 1280-atom cell, because it compares directly with the MgO results.

3. **More MgSiO3 conditions.** Everything so far is at one volume, V = 6.5669 Å³/atom (about 100–160 GPa). Do you want a second volume, for example a lower-pressure one matching X. Deng's other runs, or a denser one? My default is to finish analysing this volume first and then ask you again.

Unless you say otherwise, I'll go ahead now with:
- patching the NEB tool and resubmitting it on a P100, with nothing submitted until it's patched;
- analysing the 16 finished MgSiO3 GK runs and sweeps;
- updating INPROGRESS.md.

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Green-Kubo shear and bulk viscosity, and frequency-dependent moduli, from an NVE stress series.

Input: pres.dat written by gk_stress.lammps (fix ave/time):
    step pxx pyy pzz pxy pxz pyz temp pe etotal      (LAMMPS pressure tensor, bar)

Shear: traceless symmetric stress P^os = P - (tr P/3) I. Using all components (Daivis & Evans),
    G(t)   = V/(10 kT) sum_ab < P^os_ab(0) P^os_ab(t) >              (Eq. 1)
    eta(t) = int_0^t G(s) ds,   eta_0 = eta(t -> plateau)            (Eq. 2)
    G*(w)  = i w int_0^tc G(t) exp(-i w t) dt                        (Eq. 3)
    G'(w)  = w int G(t) sin(wt) dt,  G''(w) = w int G(t) cos(wt) dt   (Eq. 4)
    eta'(w) = G''(w)/w                                               (Eq. 5)
Bulk: p = tr P / 3,
    K_r(t) = V/kT < dp(0) dp(t) >,  zeta = int_0^tc K_r dt            (Eq. 6)
Longitudinal (relaxing part, average over the three axes):
    M_r(t) = V/kT < dP_aa(0) dP_aa(t) > = K_r(t) + 4/3 G(t)          (Eq. 7)
    M''(w) = w int M_r cos(wt) dt,  M'(w) - M_0 = w int M_r sin(wt) dt (Eq. 8)
G(0) is the infinite-frequency shear modulus G_inf (Zwanzig-Mountain, fluid).

Errors: the series is cut into NBLOCK blocks; each is analysed alone; std/sqrt(NBLOCK).
"""
import argparse
import numpy as np

kB = 1.380649e-23

def acf(x, nlag):
    """Unbiased autocorrelation of the columns of x (n, m), lags 0..nlag-1, summed over columns."""
    n = x.shape[0]
    nfft = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(2 * n)))
    f = np.fft.rfft(x, nfft, axis=0)
    c = np.fft.irfft((f * f.conj()), nfft, axis=0)[:nlag].sum(axis=1)
    return c / (n - np.arange(nlag))

def analyse(P, T, V, dt, nlag):
    """P: (n, 6) xx yy zz xy xz yz in Pa.  Returns G, K_r, M_r (Pa) at lags 0..nlag-1."""
    P = P - P.mean(axis=0)                  # fluctuations only: a solid can carry a static (residual) stress
    p = P[:, :3].mean(axis=1)
    dev = P[:, :3] - p[:, None]

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Collect all anelasticity results (oscillatory sweeps + Green-Kubo), tabulate, and plot.

Sweeps: lock-in lines in ROOT/lockin_results.txt (written by sweep_watch.sh); mean T from stress.dat.
GK:     ROOT/pres.dat analysed with gk_viscosity.analyse (block errors).

Viscosity from the slope of the loss modulus (low-frequency limit of a viscoelastic liquid):
    G''(w) = eta_0 w + O(w^3)  ->  eta_0 = lim_{w->0} dG''/dw                       (Eq. 1)
    M''(w) = (zeta_0 + 4/3 eta_0) w + O(w^3)                                         (Eq. 2)
Estimates of dG''/dw:
    secant between neighbouring sweep frequencies  (G''_{i+1} - G''_i)/(w_{i+1} - w_i)  (Eq. 3)
    weighted fit G'' = eta_0 w through the origin over f <= FMAX_FIT                 (Eq. 4)
    GK: d/dw of G''(w) = w int G(t) cos(wt) dt on a fine grid                        (Eq. 5)
Also eta'(w) = G''/w (Eq. 6) and the terminal time tau_0 = lim G'/(w G'') (Eq. 7).
Quality factor and internal friction (both channels; M for uniaxial):
    Q^-1 = tan(delta) = G''/G',  Q = G'/G''                                         (Eq. 8)
    sigma(Q^-1)^2 = (sigma_G''/G')^2 + (G'' sigma_G'/G'^2)^2,  sigma_Q = sigma(Q^-1)/Q^-2   (Eq. 9)
    For |G''| > |G'| (liquid-like, Q < 1) the same is done for Q = G'/G'' directly, sigma_Q^2 = (sigma_G'/G'')^2 + (G' sigma_G''/G''^2)^2.
    Unresolved points get 2-sigma bounds: Q > 1/(max(Q^-1,0) + 2 sigma) (loss unresolved) or Q < max(Q,0) + 2 sigma_Q (storage unresolved).
GK gives Q(w) = G'/G'' only for the liquid shear channel (equilibrium G = 0); the longitudinal GK M' lacks the
relaxed K_0, and the solid GK G' lacks the Born term, so no GK Q is given for those.

Lag correction: the stress recorded at step n is computed in the box of step n-1 (fix deform updates the box at
end_of_step), so the lock-in phase is low by exactly one MD step (perfect B1 at 5 THz: delta = -1.47 deg at
dt = 1 fs and -0.48 deg at 0.5 fs; both give +0.38 deg after the correction). Every sweep point is rotated by
    M*_corr = M*_lockin exp(i w dt_MD),  dt_MD = 1 fs                                 (Eq. 10)
i.e. M'' -> M'' cos(w dt) + M' sin(w dt), M' -> M' cos(w dt) - M'' sin(w dt). --no-lag turns it off.

Outputs in OUT: results_all.csv, results_all.md, fig_*.pdf/.png

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument('--cases', default=DEFAULT_CASES, help='case file (paths, labels, colours; see anelastic_cases_MgO_V6.6868.py)')
    ap.add_argument('--out', default=None, help='output directory (default: OUT of the case file)')
    ap.add_argument('--gk-tc', type=float, default=1.0, help='GK integration cutoff, ps')
    ap.add_argument('--fmax-fit', type=float, default=0.2, help='max f (THz) in the Eq. 4 origin fit')
    ap.add_argument('--no-lag', action='store_true', help='do not apply the one-step phase correction (Eq. 10)')
    a = ap.parse_args()
    global LAG
    if a.no_lag:
        LAG = 0.0
    globals().update({k: v for k, v in runpy.run_path(a.cases).items() if k.isupper()})
    a.out = a.out or OUT
    os.makedirs(a.out, exist_ok=True)
    style()

    S = []
    for lab, T, mode, root, tauT, valid in SWEEPS:
        rows = parse_lockin(root, mode)
        if rows:
            liquid = 'solid' not in lab
            sec, fit = slope_estimates(rows, a.fmax_fit) if valid and liquid and len(rows) > 1 else ([], (np.nan, np.nan, 0))
            S.append(dict(lab=lab, T=T, mode=mode, root=root, tauT=tauT, valid=valid, rows=rows, sec=sec, fit=fit))
    G = {k: gk_analyse(root, a.gk_tc, vbox=VBOX.get(k, NATOM * VATOM), cut_ps=GKCUT.get(k), skip_ps=GKSKIP.get(k)) for k, root in GKS}

    # ---------------- CSV of every point ----------------
    with open(f'{a.out}/results_all.csv', 'w') as fo:

                 "Mpp_over_w_mPas,dMpp_over_w_mPas,Qinv,dQinv,Q,dQ,Q_text,h2,h3\n")
        for s in S:

#!/bin/bash
# Watch anelastic sweep arrays; when a task finishes its production (PRODUCTION_STEP N of N),
# run the lock-in on its directory once and append the result to ROOT/lockin_results.txt.
# Prints one line per finished/failed task (for Monitor). Exits when no listed job is queued.
# usage: sweep_watch.sh ROOT:JOBID:MODE [ROOT:JOBID:MODE ...]
# ONESHOT=1: exit after the first loop pass that reports something (for background use).
source /resnick/home/recohen/cohen_env/bin/activate
LOCKIN=/resnick/home/recohen/Claude/tools/anelastic_lockin.py
while true; do
  active=0; reported=0
  for spec in "$@"; do
    IFS=: read ROOT JOB DEFMODE <<< "$spec"
    RES=$ROOT/lockin_results.txt
    i=0
    for line in $(grep -v '^#' $ROOT/tasks.txt | awk '{print $1":"$3":"$5":"$11}'); do
      i=$((i + 1))
      IFS=: read D P NTOT TMODE <<< "$line"
      MODE=${TMODE:-$DEFMODE}             # per-task MODE column (tasks.txt col 11) overrides ROOT:JOB:MODE
      # short runs (< 10 cycles): skip only 1/4 cycle (relaxation time << period) and use 3 blocks
      OPTS=$(awk -v n=$NTOT -v p=$P 'BEGIN{ if (n / (p * 1000) < 10) print "--skip-cycles 0.25 --nblock 3" }')
      grep -q "^$D " $RES 2>/dev/null && continue
      [ -n "$(squeue -j ${JOB}_$i -h 2>/dev/null)" ] && { active=1; continue; }
      out=$ROOT/slurm-${JOB}_$i.out
      # complete when the last PRODUCTION_STEP N of M has N >= M (whole-period chunks can overshoot M)
      if grep -h '^PRODUCTION_STEP' $out 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | awk '{exit !($2 >= $4)}'; then
        r=$(python $LOCKIN $ROOT/$D --period $P --mode $MODE $OPTS 2>&1 | grep -E "G'|M'|δ|η′|ζ|harmonics|cycles" | tr -s ' ' | tr '\n' ';')
        echo "$D $MODE P=${P}ps job ${JOB}_$i: $r" >> $RES
        echo "DONE $D ($MODE, P=$P ps): $r"; reported=1
      elif grep -qE "ERROR|CANCELLED|TIME LIMIT" $out 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "$D FAILED $(grep -hE 'ERROR|CANCELLED|TIME LIMIT' $out | head -1)" >> $RES
        echo "FAILED $D ($MODE): $(grep -hE 'ERROR|CANCELLED|TIME LIMIT' $out | head -1)"; reported=1
      elif grep -qE "^PRODUCTION_STEP" $out 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "$D INCOMPLETE $(grep -h '^PRODUCTION_STEP' $out | tail -1) -> resubmit: sbatch --array=$i sweep.sh" >> $RES
        echo "INCOMPLETE $D ($MODE): $(grep -h '^PRODUCTION_STEP' $out | tail -1); resubmit with sbatch --array=$i sweep.sh"; reported=1
      fi
    done
  done
  [ $active -eq 0 ] && { echo "ALL DONE"; exit 0; }
  [ -n "$ONESHOT" ] && [ $reported -eq 1 ] && exi

- **The onset stress barely moves.**

```
$$\delta\sigma^2\simeq C\,\frac{k_BT\,G''}{\omega VT_{run}},\qquad C\approx8 \tag{9}$$

In the viscous regime the relative error depends only on the strain-rate amplitude $\dot\gamma_0=\omega\gamma_0$. Liquid amplitudes therefore follow

$$\gamma_0=\mathrm{clip}(\dot\gamma_0/\omega,\,0.01,\,\gamma_{max}),\qquad \dot\gamma_0=10^{11}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \tag{10}$$

- $\gamma_{max}$ = 0.5 in the supercooled liquid (shear can nucleate the crystal).
- Linearity must be checked by repeating one frequency at a second amplitude. At 8000 K, γ₀ = 0.095 and 0.32 agree at 50 GHz.
- Solids use γ₀ = ε₀ = 0.01. Low-frequency defect runs use 0.02–0.03 with harmonics checked.

The cost floor is cycles, not noise: one period at frequency $f$ costs $1/(f\Delta t)$ steps, which is $10^6$ steps at 1 GHz.

### 1.5 Thermostat artefacts (uniaxial)

A Nosé–Hoover thermostat on a volume-changing cell adds a Debye relaxation between the adiabatic and isothermal moduli:
`anelastic_collect.py` tests Eq. 15 between adjacent frequencies for every crystal sweep (table §2a, `fig_kk`). The melt-grown and perfect MgO crystals agree within 1σ from 0.2 to 5 THz, which confirms that the measured loss is a linear, causal response. Expected failures:
- the bicrystal slab resonance (Eq. 13);
- heated 5 THz points (†);
- cells that drift during the sweep (unaged Schottky);
- Maxwell liquids at ωτ ≪ 1, where $G''\propto\omega$ varies quickly in ln ω and the local form does not apply, so liquids are excluded from the check.

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Build B1 MgO defect structures (LAMMPS atomic data, types 1=Mg 2=O, Maxwell velocities).

schottky : perfect n x n x n B1 cell (a = L/n) with NPAIR bound Schottky pairs removed. Each pair is a Mg site and
           its nearest-neighbour O site along a random +-x, +-y, +-z (tetragonal defect, can reorient under stress:
           Zener-type relaxation). Pair centres are kept at least DMIN apart.
bicrystal: symmetric tilt boundary Sigma5 (310)/[001]. Grain A (y < Ly/2) is the B1 lattice rotated by +theta about z,
           grain B by -theta, theta = atan(1/3) = 18.43 deg, so x || [310]_A and y || [-130]_A. Periods along x and y:
           a sqrt(10)/2; along z: a. Periodic in y, so the cell holds two boundaries. Atoms closer than RCUT across a
           boundary are removed (grain B partner); then Mg or O near the boundaries is removed to restore stoichiometry.

RCUT defaults to 0.3185 a (1.2 Å at a = 3.768 Å). A fixed RCUT does not scale with the lattice: 1.2 Å at
a = 4.256 Å leaves coincident pairs 1.35 Å apart, so always scale it with a.

Note: swapping y and z (--normal-z) is a mirror operation; B1 is centrosymmetric, so the result is an equivalent bicrystal.

usage: build_defect_crystals.py schottky  --out FILE [--a 3.767929 --n 8 --npair 20 --dmin 6 --T 5000 --seed 1]
       build_defect_crystals.py bicrystal --out FILE [--normal-z --a 3.767929 --nx 5 --ny 5 --nz 4 --rcut 0.3185a --T 5000 --seed 1]
"""
import argparse
import numpy as np

MASS = {1: 24.305, 2: 16.0}
KB = 8.617333e-5           # eV/K
CONV = 1.0364269e-4        # (g/mol)(Å/ps)^2 -> eV

def b1_cell(a):
    mg = np.array([[0, 0, 0], [0, .5, .5], [.5, 0, .5], [.5, .5, 0]])
    o = mg + np.array([.5, 0, 0])
    return np.vstack([mg, o]) * a, np.array([1] * 4 + [2] * 4)

def velocities(typ, T, rng):
    m = np.array([MASS[t] for t in typ])
    v = rng.standard_normal((len(typ), 3)) * np.sqrt(KB * T / (m[:, None] * CONV))
    v -= (m[:, None] * v).sum(0) / m.sum()
    return v

def write(fn, pos, typ, box, v, title):
    with open(fn, 'w') as f:
        f.write(f"{title}\n\n{len(typ)} atoms\n2 atom types\n\n")
        for k, ax in enumerate('xyz'):
            f.write(f"0 {box[k]:.6f} {ax}lo {ax}hi\n")
        f.write("\nMasses\n\n1 24.305\n2 16\n\nAtoms # atomic\n\n")
        for i, (p, t) in enumerate(zip(pos, typ)):
            f.write(f"{i+1} {t} {p[0]:.6f} {p[1]:.6f} {p[2]:.6f}\n")
        f.write("\nVelocities\n\n")
        for i, vv in enumerate(v):

### Claude (10-12 12:06)

Most of the analysis is done; three jobs are running and a fourth is queued.

**MgSiO3 results** (all 16 jobs, 62 sweep fits; written up as a new §5i of the results summary):
- **Liquid, cooled from 8000 K, at 129–161 GPa:**
  - **No crystallization down to 4000 K.** At 4000 K it still diffuses, so it is a deeply supercooled liquid, not a glass. MgO had already crystallized at 5000 K.
  - **Viscosity** η₀ from Green–Kubo:

    | T (K) | η₀ (mPa·s) | MgO, same T (mPa·s) |
    |---|---|---|
    | 7000 | 7.5 | 11.2 |
    | 6000 | 12.8 | 18.3 |
    | 5000 | 23 | crystallized |
    | 4000 | ~220 | crystallized |

  - The sweeps match Green–Kubo at 5000 K and above.
  - MgSiO3 is somewhat less viscous than MgO at the same T, but its viscosity climbs much faster on cooling.
  - Relative to shear viscosity, bulk viscosity is about 2.4× larger than in MgO (ζ/η ≈ 0.24 against 0.1).
  - Shear Q of the two liquids is similar. Uniaxial Q is slightly higher in MgSiO3.
- **4000 K sweep points at 10 and 50 GHz are not trustworthy.** The amplitude rule we used for MgO drove them into shear thinning, so they read about half the Green–Kubo value. A run at 5–10× smaller strain (4406967) is checking this. I added the slow-liquid rule to the methods doc.
- **Bridgmanite, heated from 2000 K, at 100–123 GPa:**
  - **It stays crystalline up to 5000 K.**
  - **Against perfect MgO at 5000 K and 1 THz:** shear Q is 63 against more than 120, so bridgmanite is lossier in shear. Uniaxial Q is 63 against 27, so it is less lossy there.
  - **Against MgO grown from the melt** (polycrystalline): bridgmanite has less loss in both channels.
  - **Near 5 THz bridgmanite has a resonance that MgO can't have.** Strain drives a lattice vibration of the distorted perovskite structure. Rock-salt MgO has no such coupling. It isn't anelasticity, so crystal comparisons use frequencies of 1 THz and below.
  - In MgO, defects and boundaries set the loss far more than the perfect lattice did, so the Mg–O vacancy cell is the comparison that matters next.

**MgO grain-boundary NEB:**
- **The first 22 h run failed in its second stage.** The climbing-image stage diverged.
- **The first stage gave a usable estimate:** about 29.5 eV, or 0.175 J/m² per boundary. That is 1.0–1.8× the small-cell barrier, not the 3× you'd expect if the whole boundary moved at once, which hints at a partly localized step.
- **The rerun (4407041) is queued, not yet started.** I hardened the tool first: it now saves the first-stage band, takes smaller and guarded steps, checkpoints, and reports where along the boundary the saddle-point motion sits. A short test run exercised all of this successfully.

**Mg–O vacancy cell in bridgmanite:**
- **Built with a new tool**, `build_vacancy_pairs.py`: 6 Mg–O vacancy pairs in 1280 atoms, the same defect density as the MgO Schottky cell. The pair sites are identical at 4000 and 5000 K.
- **200 ps aging is running** (4407170, 4407171), and I'm waiting on it. If it looks clean, I'll stage and submit the Green–Kubo runs and crystal sweeps, about 13 P100-hours.

**Docs and tools:**
- **Collector (`anelastic_collect.py`):**
  - per-case Green–Kubo cutoff;
  - liquid and crystal branches plotted separately at the same T;
  - fixed a bug that dropped the start of crystal rows in one table, and regenerated the MgO results.
- **Docs updated:** INPROGRESS, results summary §5h and §5i, methods, TODO, DONE, and a new `ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-10-12.md`.
- **Memory:** your three decisions are saved.

Results are in `results_MgSiO3_V6.5669/`; the main figure is `fig_vs_T`.

A key thing for both systems is temperature dependence. Is it an a ctivated process with a single activation energy, or possibly even temperature independent.

### Claude (10-12 12:11)

Good question. Our runs can answer it directly. All runs are at fixed volume, so "activation energy" here means the isochoric value, and pressure rises with T along each series; I'll keep that caveat in mind. My plan:
- For each quantity (liquid η₀, ζ₀ and D; crystal and liquid Q⁻¹ at fixed frequency), fit Arrhenius with one energy, a power law (T-independent is the special case n = 0), and VFT for the liquids.
- Report the local apparent energy between neighbouring temperatures. A single activation energy means that local value stays constant.

Checking what MgO data exist at both volumes.

### Claude (10-12 12:18)

For both systems, the answer is neither a single activation energy nor T-independence. The analysis is in the new results-summary §5j; the main figure is `results_Tdep/fig_T_dependence`.

**Liquids: activated, but no single activation energy.**
- **MgSiO3 viscosity:** the apparent energy rises on cooling.

  | T range (K) | apparent energy (eV) |
  |---|---|
  | 5875–7073 | 1.6 |
  | 5168–5875 | 2.2 |
  | 4035–5168 | 3.6 |

  - A single-energy (Arrhenius) fit is rejected (χ²/ν = 34).
  - A Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann (VFT) form fits within errors, with a divergence temperature of about 2800 K. Diffusion curves the same way.
  - So a single energy from the hot melt badly underestimates the viscosity at lower T.
- **MgO viscosity:** less curved. The apparent energy goes from 1.34 to 1.79 eV between 8000 and 6000 K, a 2.3σ difference. O diffusion fits a single 1.9 eV within errors.
  - MgO crystallizes before it can be supercooled, so its curvature can't be followed lower.
  - At 18–50 GPa the energy is about half (0.8 eV), so the barrier grows with compression.
- **Fixed-volume caveat:** all series are at fixed volume, so pressure rises with T. At fixed pressure the energies would be about 0.2–0.4 eV higher, judging from MgO's two volumes; the curvature is unchanged.

**Crystals at THz: not activated.**
- **Perfect bridgmanite (2000–5000 K):** loss rises in proportion to T (Q⁻¹ ∝ T^0.98±0.14), with a fitted "energy" of only 0.24 eV. That is ordinary anharmonic phonon damping, not an energy barrier.
- **MgO grown from the melt, at 18 GPa:** shear Q⁻¹ at 1 THz is T-independent within errors from 2000 to 3000 K. Its loss is dominated by freely sliding grain boundaries.
- **MgO grown from the melt, at 140 GPa:** loss rises faster than T (n ≈ 1.4), a first hint of a thermally assisted part.

**Where activation does enter: the elementary defect and grain-boundary events, and they're curved too.**
- MgO vacancy jumps fall from 3.6–4.6 eV to 2.1 eV apparent energy between 3500 and 5000 K, because the mix of jump mechanisms changes with T.
- Boundary migration at 140 GPa goes by collective steps with no single energy per area.

So at seismic frequencies the loss has to come from activated defect and boundary relaxations, and extrapolating them from high T with one activation energy isn't supported for either material.

**What I've done to fill the gaps:**
- **Bridgmanite vacancy cell at 3000 K added**, with the same defect sites as the 4000 and 5000 K cells. Its aging run (4407370) has been submitted, and the 4000 and 5000 K aging runs are still going.
- **Next, once those finish:** stage the 3000–5000 K vacancy runs, about 20 P100-hours. That gives the defect loss and vacancy hop rates against T, to compare with MgO.

**Decision for you:** MgO's perfect crystal has only been measured at one T per volume. Perfect-crystal sweeps at 3000 and 4000 K at the high-pressure volume (about 28 P100-hours) would separate MgO's phonon loss from its defect loss. Shall I submit them?

The docs, TODO, DONE and INPROGRESS are updated.

The MgO perfect-crystal runs are submitted, and the records are written.

**Submitted:**

| job | what | state |
|---|---|---|
| 4407426 | Cools the same perfect 8×8×8 lattice used at 5000 K: 20 ps at 4000 K, then 20 ps at 3000 K | running |

- They use the same task table as the 5000 K perfect-crystal sweep. The one difference is that each task re-thermalizes for 5 ps after its velocities are created, because it starts from the cooled lattice rather than from an equilibrated run.

- I didn't add Green–Kubo runs at 3000 and 4000 K. They take about 17 h each on 4096 atoms, and the sweeps give Q directly.

- **Analysis setup:** the new sweeps are already in the MgO case file. `results_Tdep/README.md` holds the exact `T_dependence.py` command.

*10-12 13:51 — context compacted*

<details><summary>10-12 13:51 — compaction summary</summary>

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - **Continue the anelasticity project for MgO and MgSiO3** (LAMMPS + DeePMD), analysing everything when jobs finish. Keep INPROGRESS.md current at every submit, finish and analysis.
   - **RC's three decisions (10-12):**
     1. Rerun the MgO 3×1 grain-boundary NEB with the fixes.
     2. Start bridgmanite defects with the Mg–O vacancy pair (V_Mg + V_O). RC will look into the perovskite grain-boundary literature, so do not build boundaries yet.
     3. Stay at V = 6.5669 Å³/atom and compare MgSiO3 with MgO.
   - **New key question from RC:** for both systems, is the temperature dependence an activated process with a single activation energy, or possibly T-independent?
   - **RC approved:** submit the MgO perfect-B1 T-series runs, and "please keep good records!"

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Oscillatory NEMD lock-in:** one-step lag correction; Green–Kubo (GK) viscosities; Q = M′/M″.
   - **Local Kramers–Kronig check.**
   - **Supercooled-liquid amplitude rule:** linear response needs γ̇₀τ_α ≪ 1. τ₀ = η/G∞ is the wrong time scale.
   - **Per-case GK cutoff:** set from the η(t) plateau (20 ps at 4000 K for MgSiO3).
   - **Bridgmanite 5 THz internal-strain resonance (summary Eq. 14).** B1 MgO has none, because every atom sits at an inversion centre.
   - **T-dependence tests:**
     - local apparent energy E_loc = s·k_B·Δln y/Δ(1/T);
     - Arrhenius, power law and VFT fits;
     - isochoric vs isobaric energy: E_P = E_V + k_B T² (∂lnη/∂p)_T (∂p/∂T)_V, about +0.35 eV for MgO (summary Eq. 15).
   - **ASE NEB with DeePMD:**
     - FIRE climbing-image divergence at maxstep 0.2 Å;
     - shared-calculator result cache;
     - saddle localization measured as the share of Σ|Δr|² in each x-slab.
   - **Vacancy-pair cells:**
     - built at the same number density as the MgO Schottky cell (6 pairs in 1280 atoms);
     - sites are chosen in a cold reference with the same atom ids, so cells at every T carry identical defects.
   - **Job mechanics:**

return t

def read_gk(d):
    rows = []
    for l in open(os.path.join(d, 'results_gk.csv')):
        if l.startswith('#'):
            continue
        w = l.rstrip('\n').split(',')
        rows.append(dict(key=w[0], T=float(w[1]), p=float(w[2]), run=float(w[3]), liq=w[5] == '1',
                         eta=float(w[7]), deta=float(w[8]), zeta=float(w[9]), dzeta=float(w[10]), root=w[13]))
    return rows

def diffusion(root, run_ps, nblk=3):
    """D (1e-9 m^2/s) per species from msd.dat (step, msd_1..): slope over the second half of [0, run_ps]."""
    fn = os.path.join(root, 'msd.dat')
    if not os.path.exists(fn):
        return None
    m = np.loadtxt(fn); t = m[:, 0] * 1e-3                      # ps (1 fs steps)
    sel = (t >= 0.5 * run_ps) & (t <= run_ps); t, m = t[sel], m[sel, 1:]
    D = np.polyfit(t, m, 1)[0] / 6 * 10                          # Å^2/ps /6 -> 1e-8 m^2/s; x10 -> 1e-9
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(len(t)), nblk)
    Db = np.array([np.polyfit(t[b], m[b], 1)[0] / 6 * 10 for b in blocks])
    return D, Db.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(nblk)

def read_q(d, sub):
    out = {}
    for r in csv.reader(open(os.path.join(d, 'results_all.csv'))):
        if not r or r[0] != 'sweep' or sub not in r[5] or r[4] != 'True':
            continue
        f = float(r[6]); key = (r[2], round(f / 1e9))
        out.setdefault(key, []).append((float(r[8]), float(r[15]), float(r[16])))
    return out

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Temperature dependence of transport and loss: single activation energy, curved (super- or sub-Arrhenius), or
T-independent? Reads the outputs of anelastic_collect.py (results_gk.csv, results_all.csv) for several cases and the
GK msd.dat files.

Series (fixed V each, so p rises with T; energies are isochoric):
    liquid  eta_0, zeta_0 (GK), self-diffusion D_i = slope(MSD_i)/6 (second half of the GK run, <= run_ps)
    crystal Q^-1 = M''/M' at fixed f (0.2 and 1 THz, lag-corrected sweeps; rows of results_all.csv whose directory
            contains --crystal-dir, default FreqSweep_solid)
Tests, for y(T):
    local apparent energy  E_loc = s k_B d ln y / d(1/T)  between neighbouring T     (Eq. 1)
        (s = +1 for eta, zeta; s = -1 for D, rates and Q^-1, so E_loc > 0 means 'activated, faster when hot')
    Arrhenius              ln y = a + s E/(k_B T),  chi^2/dof                          (Eq. 2)
    power law              ln y = a + n ln T,       chi^2/dof  (n = 0: T-independent)   (Eq. 3)
    VFT (>= 4 points)      ln y = a + s B/(T - T_0)                                    (Eq. 4)
A single activation energy means E_loc is constant within errors and Eq. 2 fits (chi^2/dof ~ 1).

## 5j. Temperature dependence: one activation energy, curved, or T-independent? (2026-10-12)

**Method.** `tools/T_dependence.py` runs on `results_gk.csv` (new collector output) and `results_all.csv` for all three cases, giving `results_Tdep/{T_dependence.md,.csv}` and `fig_T_dependence`. For each quantity y(T) it computes:
- the local apparent energy between neighbouring temperatures, $E_{loc}=s\,k_B\,\Delta\ln y/\Delta(1/T)$, with s = +1 for η, ζ and s = −1 for D and $Q^{-1}$;
- a single-E Arrhenius fit;
- a power law $y\propto T^n$, where n = 0 means T-independent;
- for 4 or more points, VFT, $\ln y=a+sB/(T-T_0)$.

All series are at fixed V, so the energies are **isochoric**. The isobaric value is larger:

$$E_P=E_V+k_BT^2\left(\frac{\partial\ln\eta}{\partial p}\right)_T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V \tag{15}$$

For liquid MgO at 6000 K the two volumes give $(\partial\ln\eta/\partial p)_T$ = 0.013 GPa⁻¹ (activation volume ≈ 1.1 Å³). With $(\partial p/\partial T)_V$ = 8.4 MPa/K, $E_P-E_V\approx$ 0.35 eV. The correction grows only as T², so it shifts the energies below by about 0.2–0.4 eV without changing their curvature.

**1. Liquids: no single activation energy. Both melts are super-Arrhenius, and MgSiO₃ strongly so.**

### Claude (10-13 07:55)

I ran T_dependence.py on every series and wrote the results file at `Anelasticity/results_Tdep/T_DEPENDENCE_RESULTS.md`.

All of yesterday's jobs had finished, so I first ran the lock-ins on the new sweeps and the collectors for MgSiO₃ and MgO. I also had to fix one thing in the tool: the perfect and vacancy bridgmanite sweeps both live in directories called `FreqSweep_solid`, and the old version would have fitted them together as one series. A new `--series` option keeps them apart, and `--defect-gk` adds the vacancy-cell diffusion from the 1.5 ns GK runs.

**Answer to your question (single activation energy, or T-independent?)**

1. **Liquids:** activated, but not with one energy.
   - MgSiO₃ is strongly curved: the apparent energy for viscosity rises from 1.6 to 3.6 eV on cooling, a single-E fit is rejected (χ²/ν = 34), and VFT fits with T₀ ≈ 2800 K.
   - MgO is mildly curved, 1.3 to 1.8 eV.
2. **Perfect crystals at THz:** not activated.
   - MgO perfect B1, 3000–5000 K (new): uniaxial Q⁻¹ at 1 THz goes as T^(1.22 ± 0.11). The formal energy of 0.40 eV is far below any barrier, so this is phonon damping.
   - MgO uniaxial loss at 0.2 THz is **T-independent** (n = 0.2 ± 0.4, Q⁻¹ ≈ 0.014). Akhiezer damping would explain that, but I haven't checked it independently.
   - MgO C₄₄ shear loss is unresolved at every T (Q > 300).
   - Perfect bridgmanite goes as Q⁻¹ ∝ T^1.0.
3. **Bridgmanite with V_Mg + V_O pairs, 3000–5000 K (new):**
   - **Loss at 1 THz:** the vacancy cells are 25–60 % lossier than the perfect crystal at 4000–5000 K, but each difference is only about 1σ, so the defect THz loss is not resolved.
   - **O vacancies** jump at about 5×10⁹ to 2×10¹¹ s⁻¹. One activation energy fits, E = 2.36 ± 0.12 eV (isochoric), but three points make that a weak test. In MgO the vacancy energies are curved.
   - **Mg vacancies** are frozen below 5000 K on ns time scales. In MgO, Mg vacancies move about as fast as O vacancies.
   - **Si moves at 5000 K** even though the cell has no Si vacancies, possibly antisites or Frenkel defects. I haven't analysed this yet.

**Bottom line:** in both minerals the THz crystal loss is phonon loss, either linear in T or T-independent. The activated processes are the vacancy jumps. For a seismic-band comparison the missing piece is the bridgmanite vacancy loss below 50 GHz; MgO's large defect loss only appeared at 20–50 GHz.

**Two other jobs finished:**
- **MgSiO₃ 4000 K linearity test:** η′ = 114 mPa s at 50 GHz and 202 at 10 GHz, against 220 from GK. This confirms the earlier low values came from too large an amplitude. Summary §5i isn't updated yet.
- **MgO 3×1 grain-boundary NEB rerun:** finished in under 3 hours; I haven't looked at the output yet.

INPROGRESS lists both as pending analysis. I have also updated summary §5j, the DONE log, the methods tool table and `results_Tdep/README.md`, which has the exact command.

Decision for you: the results file proposes three next steps — bridgmanite vacancy sweeps at 50 and 20 GHz, a site analysis of the Si motion at 5000 K, and static barriers for the bridgmanite vacancies. Do you want me to submit the sweeps?

### Claude (10-13 08:01)

I submitted the bridgmanite V_Mg + V_O shear sweeps at 50 and 20 GHz, at 4000 K (job 4446443) and 5000 K (job 4446444). Both are still waiting in the queue, so I haven't yet seen a task start.

The setup copies the aged MgO Schottky low-frequency runs, so the two systems can be compared directly:
- **Starting point:** the end of each temperature's 1.5 ns Green–Kubo run, with new velocities and then 100 ps of constant-temperature equilibration. The vacancies will have aged about 1.7 ns in total.
- **Drive:** shear at strain amplitude 0.02, twice the amplitude of the 1 THz runs, because loss signals are smaller at low frequency.
- **Length:** 40 cycles at 50 GHz (period 20 ps) and 20 cycles at 20 GHz (period 50 ps).
- **Cost:** about 3.6 GPU-hours per run, about 15 in total. They start from the vacancy cells' own sweep script, so the masses and model settings are the same as before.

When they finish I'll compare against two things:
- **Perfect bridgmanite at 50 GHz.** Is there a vacancy loss we can now resolve?
- **The aged MgO vacancy cell.** There Q was 9.7 at 50 GHz and 3.7 at 20 GHz at 5000 K. The main question is whether the bridgmanite loss also rises toward low frequency.

The job IDs and exact settings are written up in four places:
- **Run README:** `V6.5669/crystal_VMgO/README.md`
- **Tracking docs:** INPROGRESS.md (with the commands to run when the jobs finish) and ANELASTICITY_DONE.md
- **Results file:** a note in `results_Tdep/T_DEPENDENCE_RESULTS.md` §4
- **Case file:** `anelastic_cases_MgSiO3_V6.5669.py` now lists the new runs; they are included automatically once their results exist.

Abstract. Theoretical calculations of diffusion in periclase

Nature  |  Vol 613  |  12 January 2023  |  303
Article
Periclase deforms more slowly than 
bridgmanite under mantle conditions
Patrick Cordier1,2 ✉, Karine Gouriet1, Timmo Weidner1, James Van Orman3, Olivier Castelnau4, 
Jennifer M. Jackson5 & Philippe Carrez1
Transport of heat from the interior of the Earth drives convection in the mantle, 
which involves the deformation of solid rocks over billions of years. The lower  
mantle of the Earth is mostly composed of iron-bearing bridgmanite MgSiO3 and 
approximately 25% volume periclase MgO (also with some iron). It is commonly 
accepted that ferropericlase is weaker than bridgmanite1. Considerable progress has 
been made in recent years to study assemblages representative of the lower mantle 
under the relevant pressure and temperature conditions2,3. However, the natural 
strain rates are 8 to 10 orders of magnitude lower than in the laboratory, and are still 
inaccessible to us. Once the deformation mechanisms of rocks and their constituent 
minerals have been identified, it is possible to overcome this limitation thanks to 
multiscale numerical modelling, and to determine rheological properties for 
inaccessible strain rates. In this work we use 2.5-dimensional dislocation dynamics  
to model the low-stress creep of MgO periclase at lower mantle pressures and 
temperatures. We show that periclase deforms very slowly under these conditions,  
in particular, much more slowly than bridgmanite deforming by pure climb creep.

Seismic anisotropy in the Earth’s lower mantle, particularly around subduction zones, is commonly
attributed to deformation by dislocation creep, yet much of the lower mantle appears nearly isotropic.
This contrast complicates interpretations of mantle rheology. Here we report the temperature
dependence of lattice preferred orientation in bridgmanite, the most abundant lower mantle mineral,
through high-pressure deformation experiments at 25 gigapascals and 1700–2100 kelvin. Both iron-
free and iron-bearing bridgmanite develop lattice preferred orientations across this temperature range,
with distinct slip systems occurring below and above 1800 kelvin. Low-temperature fabric produces
strong seismic anisotropy, whereas high-temperature fabric yields weak, near-isotropic signatures
under horizontal shearing. These results provide a uniﬁed explanation for strong seismic anisotropy
near subduction zones and globally near-isotropic behavior of the lower mantle. They suggest that
dislocation creep could dominate lower mantle deformation while generating diverse seismic
signatures, providing important understanding for lower mantle rheology and dynamics.

## 5a. Vacancy jump rates from MD (T17 step 1)

Setup:
- **Cell:** 20-pair Schottky cell at $V$ = 6.6868 Å³/atom (138–148 GPa); NVT, 200 ps at each T, positions every 0.1 ps (`DefectHops/<T>K`, job 4238025).
- **Analysis:** `tools/vacancy_hops.py` assigns atoms to Wigner–Seitz sites on the ideal lattice.
- **Rate estimate:** the jump rate per vacancy comes from on-lattice tracer diffusion, which is free of recrossings,

$$\Gamma_v=\frac{6D^*}{f\,c_v\,\lambda^2},\qquad \lambda=\frac{a}{\sqrt2},\quad f=0.78 \tag{8}$$

  Here $c_v$ is the vacancy site fraction. Direct hop counts depend on the minimum residence time chosen, so they are printed only as a check.

| T (K) | p (GPa) | $D^*_{Mg}$ (Å²/ps) | $D^*_{O}$ (Å²/ps) | $\Gamma_{Mg}$ (ps⁻¹) | $\Gamma_{O}$ (ps⁻¹) | vacancies Mg/O (mean) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3501 | 138.2 | 1.8×10⁻⁴ | 8.4×10⁻⁵ | 0.020 | 0.0093 | 20.1 / 20.1 |
| 4003 | 141.7 | 8.4×10⁻⁴ | 5.8×10⁻⁴ | 0.089 | 0.062 | 20.7 / 20.5 |
| 4505 | 144.9 | 2.0×10⁻³ | 1.6×10⁻³ | 0.195 | 0.156 | 23.0 / 22.5 |
| 5004 | 148.3 | 3.8×10⁻³ | 2.8×10⁻³ | 0.337 | 0.265 | 24.6 / 23.7 |

- **Mechanism:** more than 95 % of jumps go to the nearest same-sublattice site, along ⟨110⟩ at a distance $a/\sqrt2$. Second-neighbour ⟨100⟩ and longer jumps rise with T, to about 4 % at 5000 K.
- **Not a single activation energy.** The local apparent $E_a=-k_B\,d\ln\Gamma/d(1/T)$ falls steeply with T:

| interval (K) | $E_a$, Mg (eV) | $E_a$, O (eV) |
|---|---|---|
| 3500–4000 | 3.61 | 4.57 |
| 4000–4500 | 2.42 | 2.84 |
| 4500–5000 | 2.12 | 2.08 |

  A single Arrhenius fit (2.84 eV for Mg, 3.38 eV for O) misses the 3500 K points. Statistical error at 3500 K is about ±13 % (about 55 O hops, 136 Mg hops), so the curvature is well beyond noise (`results/fig_vacancy_arrhenius`).
- **Likely causes of the curvature:**
  - extra thermally generated defects above 4500 K (up to 36 vacancies and 5–8 atoms in flight per frame);
  - vacancy clustering and binding (PE drifts by 20–50 eV over the run);
  - anharmonic and entropic softening of the barrier near melting.

  Static (NEB) barriers at the same volume, the next step, will separate these effects.
- **Consequence for extrapolation:** an activation energy fitted at high T underestimates relaxation times at lower T. Here it would be off by a factor of about 3 already at 3500 K, for oxygen.

### Claude (10-13 09:03)

I've read the papers and written the plan: `ANELASTICITY_PLAN_FE_DISLOCATIONS.md` (TODO T20–T22). Here is what bears on it:

**Cordier et al. 2023 (s41586-022-05410-9).** Their claim that "periclase deforms more slowly than bridgmanite" rests on the Ita & Cohen O-diffusion fit for MgO. On the bridgmanite side they assume a vacancy fraction of 10⁻⁵.
- Repeating the Ita & Cohen free-energy calculation with DeePMD for both minerals, using one model, tests their conclusion directly.
- Their Table 1 has a typo: E₀ = 0.4×10⁻¹⁹ J should be 9.4×10⁻¹⁹ J. With 9.4, I reproduce their Table 2 D values within 5 %.

**Ita & Cohen method.** All the pieces are in our GPU LAMMPS build:
- `fix ti/spring` does the same switching to an Einstein crystal, with the same λ(t) polynomial as their Eq. 6.
- PLUMED is linked, for the migration free-energy profiles.
- X. Deng's MgSiO₃ model was trained on both bridgmanite and MgO from 20 to 160 GPa. So one model can give consistent formation energies for both minerals, including the MgO chemical potential needed for MgO-type vacancy pairs in bridgmanite.

**A correction to our own results.** Summary §5c says thermal Schottky pairs should appear near 5000 K, based on a 2.44 eV energy computed at fixed volume.
- That number leaves out the P·v_f term in Ita & Cohen's Eq. 3, which is about 12–16 eV at 140–190 GPa. Their bound-pair formation energy is 13–17 eV.
- So thermal Schottky pairs should not form in our runs. The extra vacancies we saw above 4500 K must be Frenkel pairs.
- The same problem applies to yesterday's "≈ 1.9 eV per pair" for bridgmanite.
- I've added correction notes to §5c and the vacancy-cell README.

**Perez et al. 2025.** They put an upper bound of about 100 Pa s on solid MgO viscosity at 175 GPa, about 3500 K and strain rates of 10⁶–10⁷ s⁻¹. That is close to our V6.6868 conditions.
- If dislocations glide with only drag resisting them, the effective viscosity is η = B/(ρb²). Here B is the drag coefficient, ρ the dislocation density and b the Burgers vector.
- Plausible drag coefficients give about 10 Pa s, so computing B directly from MD is a clean test of their bound.
- The same B gives the dislocation (Granato–Lücke) loss peak. That could be the seismic-band loss source that vacancies don't provide.

**Guan et al. 2026.** MD can measure the critical resolved shear stress of [100](010) and [010](100) against temperature, and so test whether they cross near 1800 K.
- Guan's data are at 25 GPa, which is inside the Deng model's training range.
- This is the most expensive part: cells of 30–60 thousand atoms, about 300–400 GPU-hours.

The whole program is about 650–750 GPU-hours. I'd start with an ≈8 GPU-hour test of the free-energy setup against Ita & Cohen's MgO numbers. I need a few decisions first:

### Claude (10-13 10:14)

Agreed. I'll start the MgO dislocation work for the Perez comparison (plan phase B1) now, alongside the free-energy test.

I'll use the MgO-only model here, not Deng's. Perez's 175 GPa is above Deng's 160 GPa training limit, while the MgO model is the one from our 175–193 GPa (V6.6868) anelasticity runs.

The method is the standard one for dislocation mobility:
- **Cell:** a periodic slab with one ½[110](001) edge dislocation, made by joining a block of N+1 lattice repeats to one of N.
- **Loading:** rigid top and bottom blocks act as a piston, which supplies the 175 GPa normal stress.
- **Drag:** a fixed shear force on the top block drives the dislocation, and its speed comes from the plastic slip of the top block, giving the drag coefficient B = bτ/v.

I'll check the MgO model's type map first.

### Claude (10-13 10:17)

Yes, I've started the Perez comparison. A short smoke test is queued alongside the free-energy one; no MgO dislocation results yet.

**Model:** I'm using the MgO-only model from our V6.6868 anelasticity runs, not Deng's. Perez's 175 GPa is above the 160 GPa limit of Deng's training data, while the MgO model is already in use at 140–193 GPa.

**Setup:**
- The cell is a slab containing one ½[110](001) edge dislocation, the slip system expected above about 50 GPa. It has 8232 atoms and is periodic along the glide direction and the dislocation line.
- Rigid top and bottom blocks act as a piston to supply the 175 GPa normal stress, and a lateral force on the top block applies the shear stress τ.
- The dislocation speed v comes from how fast the top block slides: it moves one Burgers vector b each time the dislocation crosses the cell. That gives the drag coefficient B = bτ/v.
- The effective viscosity is then η_eff = B/(ρb²) for dislocation densities ρ = 10¹³–10¹⁶ m⁻², compared with Perez's bound of η ≤ 100 Pa s.
- The lowest τ that moves the dislocation bounds the lattice resistance at 3500 K, to compare with their yield strength of about 1 GPa or less.

**New tools:** `build_mgo_edge_slab.py`, `npt_lattice.lammps`, `disl_drive.lammps`, `disl_job.sh` and `disl_velocity.py`, all in `tools/`.

**Queued:**
- **Dislocation smoke test (4450669):** a bulk NPT run for the lattice parameter at 175 GPa / 3500 K, the slab build, and two τ values, in `Downloads/disltest`.
- **Free-energy smoke test (4450400):** still waiting in the queue.

If the dislocation smoke test passes, I'll start the production run in `LAMMPS/MgO/Dislocations/edge_P175_T3500`, with a README: τ = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 GPa, about 3–4 GPU-hours. Screw dislocations and 2000 / 5000 K come after that. The plan (§3a) and INPROGRESS are updated.

### Claude (10-13 11:01)

Both production runs are submitted, after each smoke test passed:

- **Perez comparison, job 4452807:**
  - **Setup:** one MgO ½[110](001) edge dislocation in an 8232-atom slab, at 175 GPa and 3500 K. NPT gives a lattice parameter of 3.704 Å at those conditions.
  - **Drive:** shear stresses of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 GPa, 30 ps each.
  - **Cost:** about 2 GPU-hours.
  - **Output:** dislocation speed v(τ), drag coefficient B and effective viscosity η_eff, compared with Perez's bound of η ≤ 100 Pa s.
  - **Record:** `LAMMPS/MgO/Dislocations/edge_P175_T3500/README.md`.
- **Free-energy check, job 4452757:**
  - **Runs:** six, covering perfect and bound vacancy-pair MgO at 20 GPa / 2000 K and 140 GPa / 3000 K, plus a switching-time check.
  - **Comparison:** Ita & Cohen got 7.51 and 15.79 eV for the bound pair at those two points.

Each smoke test failed once before passing, and both causes are fixed:
- **Free energy:** the averaging command wouldn't take unwrapped coordinates.
- **Dislocation:** the DeePMD model needed a different per-atom stress command.

INPROGRESS and DONE are updated. I'll analyse both runs when they finish.

        - do Ita & Cohen-style free-energy integrations for vacancy formation free energies and diffusion rates;
        - put in dislocations (bridgmanite slip systems per Guan).
     d) Compare every result with previous work.
     e) Pursue the comparison with Perez on MgO.
   - **RC decisions (AskUserQuestion answers):**
     - Ita grid plus Cordier geotherm points;
     - all three bridgmanite Schottky types;
     - "Is Deng's model trained on MgO? If so 1." (verified yes, so use the Deng model for both minerals);
     - dislocations at 25 GPa plus V6.5669.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Frenkel–Ladd nonequilibrium TI:**
     - LAMMPS `fix ti/spring` with `function 2`, the de Koning λ(t) (= Ita Eq. 6); forward/backward switching.
     - F = F_E − (W_f − W_b)/2, with F_E = 3kT Σ ln(ħω/kT) plus a fixed-COM correction; k_s = 3kT/⟨Δr²⟩.
     - ΔG_f = F_D − (N−L)/N F_I + P[V_D − (N−L)/N V_I] (Ita Eq. 3).
   - **Migration:** PMF along the jump coordinate via PLUMED (`fix plumed` is linked; colvars is absent); TST rate Γ = ν* exp(−ΔG_m/kT).
   - **Diffusion and fit:** D from Ita Eq. 1; Cordier's fit Eq. 10 (ln D = ln(a²ν) + (S0+PS0′)/kB − (E0+PV0+P²V0′)/kBT).
   - **Chemical potentials for partial Schottky defects:** μ_MgO = g_per; μ_SiO2 = g_Bdm − g_per.
   - **Dislocation mobility (Osetsky–Bacon two-block slab):**
     - edge from NX+1 vs NX repeats;
     - rigid top/bottom blocks; piston normal force −P·A;
     - shear τ applied as force on the top block (addforce + aveforce);
     - v = (d dx_top/dt)·Lx/b; B = bτ/v; η_eff = B/(ρb²) (Orowan);
     - Granato–Lücke damping τ_d = BL²/(π²C).
   - **T-dependence tests:** E_loc, Arrhenius, power law, VFT; Akhiezer damping (T-independent Q⁻¹ when ωτ ≪ 1).
   - **Hop rates:** Γ_v ≈ 6 D_i N_i/(n_v ℓ²).
