### Claude (10-13 17:38)

Two of the three batches have finished, and the free-energy test gives clearly lower vacancy energies than Ita & Cohen; the dislocation run is still going.

**Free-energy test (job 4452757) – finished, first analysis done.** These are formation energies for a bound Mg–O vacancy pair in MgO:

| state | switching time | ΔG_f (eV) | formation volume (Ω) | Ita & Cohen (eV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 GPa, 2000 K | 40 ps | 5.15 ± 0.21 | 1.32 | 7.51 |
| 140 GPa, 3000 K | 40 ps | 11.90 ± 0.24 | 0.97 | 15.79 |
| 140 GPa, 3000 K | 20 ps | 12.68 ± 0.31 | 1.09 | 15.79 |

- **No atom jumps:** the largest displacement from its site was ≤ 1.0 Å in every run, so the method behaved.
- **The two switching times disagree by 0.8 eV.** The free-energy part agrees to 0.12 eV. The gap is in the P·ΔV term, because the formation volume is not yet well averaged. Longer pressure-controlled averaging or more replicas will fix that.
- **The Deng model is about 30 % below Ita & Cohen** (2.4 and 3.9 eV lower). I don't know why yet. It could be the potential itself or a difference in how the bound pair is defined. The next checks are a separated pair and a DFT spot check.

**Bridgmanite vacancy sweeps at 50 and 20 GHz (jobs 4446443 and 4446444) – finished, not yet analysed.** Next I'll collect the lock-in results and compare them with perfect bridgmanite and with aged MgO (Q 9.7 at 50 GHz, 3.7 at 20 GHz).

**MgO edge dislocation for the Perez comparison (job 4452807) – running, about 1 h in.** It is in the second of four stress steps (τ = 0.25 GPa); the whole run should take about 2 h.
- **First step (τ = 0.1 GPa):** the dislocation moves at about 320 ± 80 m/s, giving a drag coefficient B ≈ 8×10⁻⁵ Pa s.
- **Effective viscosity:** with dislocation densities of 10¹³ to 10¹⁶ m⁻², η_eff ranges from about 120 down to 0.1 Pa s. That is the same order as Perez's bound of η ≤ 100 Pa s, but it is preliminary.
- **Pressure is short:** the normal stress in the slab averages about 168 GPa rather than the target 175 GPa. I'll check how the piston force is set before the follow-up runs.

I've recorded the free-energy results in that run's README, and INPROGRESS.md is updated for all three jobs.

### Claude (10-13 17:47)

I've set up the DFT spot check of the Deng model. The first step, a short DeePMD run (job 4480280) that makes snapshots to send to VASP, is in the queue; no DFT results yet.

**Matching the model's own DFT.** VASP is the right code because Deng's training data are VASP. Their inputs are in `XDeng/MgSiO/MLP/inputs/MgO/`, and I'm reusing them unchanged:
- **Functional:** PBEsol (`GGA = PS`), not PBE.
- **Pseudopotentials:** standard PAW Mg and O.
- **Other settings:** 800 eV cutoff, Fermi smearing at k_BT.
- **Cells:** 128-atom cells on a 2×2×2 Γ mesh in training. I use Γ only on the 512-atom cells, which gives the same k-point density.

Comparing against the model's own DFT tells us how much of the 2.4–3.9 eV gap is model error rather than real physics.

**Part 1: snapshots of the actual TI cells.** The snapshots come from the free-energy cells themselves: perfect (512 atoms) and bound pair (510 atoms), at 20 GPa/2000 K and 140 GPa/3000 K, 8 frames each.
- **Per frame:** VASP energy, pressure and forces go side by side with DeePMD's.
- **ΔE = E_DFT − E_DP:** a perturbation estimate from the bound-pair and perfect cells gives the model's error in ΔG_f directly.
- **ΔP at fixed volume:** this is the EOS error you raised. It tells us whether the model puts MgO at the wrong volume at a given P and T.
- **Order of runs:** one test frame first, then an array of 32 frames at 64 cores each. I estimate under an hour per frame, but the test run will pin that down.

**Part 2, next: static relaxed formation enthalpies.** DFT and DeePMD in 64- and 216-atom cells at 0, 20 and 140 GPa, for both the bound and separated pair. These can be compared directly with published static DFT values (e.g. Karki & Khanduja 2006).

I've added four new tools under `~/Claude/tools`: `dft_snapshots.lammps`, `dft_snapshots_poscar.py`, `vasp_array.sh` and `dft_compare.py`. The run directory is `rcohen/VASP/MgO_vacancy_DFTcheck/`, with a README, and INPROGRESS.md has a new row.

I'm using VASP rather than Quantum ESPRESSO because it reproduces the training reference exactly. A QE cross-check would only separate PAW differences from model error, so I'd keep it for later if the gap turns out large.

### Claude (10-13 18:12)

The snapshot run finished, and I've submitted a one-frame VASP test (job 4482343). It's the bound pair at 140 GPa and 3000 K on 32 cores, there to measure run time and memory before the full set.

- **Snapshots:** 32 frames in 8 minutes: perfect and bound-pair cells at 20 GPa/2000 K and 140 GPa/3000 K, 8 frames each.
- **Pressures:** DeePMD gives about 17 and 134 GPa without the kinetic term; adding it brings these to the target 20 and 140 GPa. These numbers without the kinetic term are what the VASP stress will be compared against.
- **VASP inputs:** all 32 frame directories are built. The INCAR is Deng's training file with only these changes:
  - smearing width set to k_BT (0.2585 eV at 3000 K);
  - NCORE = 8;
  - comment and blank lines stripped.

  Everything else (PBEsol, standard Mg and O PAW, 800 eV cutoff) is unchanged.

Once the test returns cleanly, I'll submit the other 31 frames as an array on 2 nodes × 32 cores. Then `dft_compare.py` gives the DFT − DeePMD error in vacancy-pair formation energy and in pressure at each state. The README and INPROGRESS are updated.

### Claude (10-13 18:43)

The MgO edge-dislocation run for the Perez comparison (4452807) has finished. It gives a drag coefficient B = 2.2×10⁻⁴ Pa s at 175 GPa and 3500 K, which is consistent with Perez's η ≤ 100 Pa s.

| τ (GPa) | v (m/s) | B (Pa s) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 316 ± 78 | not steady glide |
| 0.25 | 50 ± 108 | stalls |
| 0.50 | 585 ± 97 | 2.2×10⁻⁴ |
| 1.00 | 1170 ± 135 | 2.2×10⁻⁴ |

- **High stress:** at 0.5 and 1 GPa the dislocation glides steadily, with velocity proportional to stress.
- **Effective viscosity:** with dislocation densities from 10¹³ to 10¹⁶ m⁻², η_eff = B/(ρb²) runs from 330 down to 0.33 Pa s.
- **Against Perez:** drag alone gives η below 100 Pa s for any density above about 3×10¹³ m⁻². But then drag alone cannot give their GPa-level strength at 10⁷ s⁻¹; that needs either a low density or a resistance other than drag.
- **Low stress:** at 0.25 GPa or below there is no steady glide. That fits a lattice-friction or pinning threshold between 0.25 and 0.5 GPa, which would be the extra resistance. It could also just be that 30 ps is too short; 100 ps runs at 0.25–0.5 GPa will tell.
- **Checks:**
  - Temperature held at 3500 K throughout.
  - The shear stress in the slab tracks the applied stress.
  - The normal stress reads about 167–170 GPa against the 175 GPa target. I suspect my rough estimate of the slab volume in the stress calculation rather than the piston force. A perfect slab under the same piston will settle it.

The plot is `edge_velocity.pdf/.png` in the run directory. I added a `--plot` option to `disl_velocity.py` to make it.

The README, INPROGRESS, DONE and the 10-13 restart are all updated.

The VASP test job (4482343) is still waiting in the queue. Once it has run cleanly, the 32-frame DFT array goes in.

**Next:**
- 100 ps runs at 0.25–0.5 GPa to settle the threshold;
- the perfect-slab stress check;
- a screw dislocation;
- 2000 and 5000 K;
- a size check with a box twice as long in the glide direction.

  - Solid single-crystal MgO has an effective viscosity of at most about $10^2$ Pa s at 175 ± 15 GPa, about 3500 K and $\dot\varepsilon=10^6$–$10^7$ s⁻¹. That implies a flow stress of about 1 GPa or less.
  - The conditions are close to our V6.6868 MgO crystal (140–190 GPa).
  - In the athermal glide regime, a drag-controlled dislocation population has the Newtonian effective viscosity of Eq. 12 below. MD can compute the drag coefficient $B$ at these conditions.
- **Correction to our own records (summary §5c, and the bridgmanite "≈ 1.9 eV per pair" note in `crystal_VMgO/README.md`).**
  - The fixed-V quantity $E(N-2)-\frac{N-2}{N}E_{perf}$ (2.44 eV in MgO) leaves out the $P\,v_f$ term of Eq. 3 below. At 140–190 GPa that term is of order $P\cdot2\Omega\approx$ 12–16 eV.
  - Ita & Cohen's bound-pair $\Delta G_f$ is 13–17 eV at 80–140 GPa.
  - Thermal Schottky pairs are therefore **not** expected near 5000 K. The extra vacancies seen above 4500 K in fixed-N MD (§5a, "atoms in flight") must be Frenkel pairs.

- **Effective viscosity:** $\\eta_{eff}=B/(\\rho b^2)$ = 330, 33, 3.3 and 0.33 Pa s for ρ = 10¹³, 10¹⁴, 10¹⁵ and 10¹⁶ m⁻².
  - This meets Perez's η ≤ 10² Pa s for ρ ≳ 3 × 10¹³ m⁻², or about 10¹⁴ m⁻² with orientation factors.
  - Drag-limited flow stress at 10⁷ s⁻¹ is ≤ 0.33 GPa for ρ ≥ 10¹⁴ m⁻², so the ≲ 1 GPa strength is set by the threshold, not drag.
- **Granato–Lücke:** with this B, string damping (plan Eq. 13) peaks at 7 kHz for L = 100 µm and needs L ≈ 1 cm for 1 Hz. Drag-controlled dislocation loss is not a seismic-band mechanism; kink-pair or pinning processes w

### Claude (10-13 19:05)

The write-up is at `Anelasticity/results_dislocations/MGO_EDGE_DISLOCATION_RESULTS.md`. Its main finding is that drag on the MgO edge dislocation easily explains a viscosity as low as Perez measured.

- **Drag:** at 175 GPa and 3500 K, B = 2.2×10⁻⁴ Pa s, from steady glide at 0.5 and 1 GPa. Below 0.25 GPa the dislocation does not glide steadily.
- **Viscosity against Perez:**
  - Perez's bound of η ≤ 100 Pa s is met for any mobile dislocation density above about 3×10¹³ m⁻², or about 10¹⁴ m⁻² once orientation factors are included. Shocked crystals usually have more than that.
  - At those densities, drag alone gives a flow stress ≤ 0.33 GPa at 10⁷ s⁻¹. So the ≲ 1 GPa strength Perez implies would come from the 0.25–0.5 GPa threshold, if the longer runs show it is real, not from drag.
  - Both are far below the 7.5–15 GPa extrapolated static strengths.
- **Seismic loss:** with this B, damping of pinned dislocation segments peaks at about 7 kHz for 100 µm segments. Reaching 1 Hz would need about 1 cm free segments.
  - So drag cannot be the source of seismic-band dislocation loss; that would have to be a slower process, such as kink-pair formation or pinning and unpinning.
  - This estimate assumes a shear modulus of about 300 GPa at 175 GPa, which I haven't checked against our runs.

The document has the method and Eqs. 1–6, the results table and figure, the comparison table against Perez with its caveats, the next steps, and the commands to reproduce.

One check is still open: the slab's normal stress reads about 168 GPa rather than 175. A perfect slab under the same piston will settle it.

I also added a short summary as §5k of `ANELASTICITY_RESULTS_SUMMARY.md` and updated DONE and the restart.

I can also publish the write-up as a private web page you could share, if that would help.

### Claude (10-13 19:45)

The VASP test (job 4482343) failed in 14 seconds without computing anything, because of a library mismatch.

- **Cause:** `~/bin/vasp_gam` is linked against oneAPI 2025.3, which provides MKL `.so.2`. The `load_intel` alias now loads oneAPI 2026.1, which only provides MKL `.so.3`.
- **Fix:** `vasp_array.sh` now sources `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh` (2025.3), the same environment Deng's training jobs used. With it, `ldd` resolves every library.
- **Binary:** it contains no WSDA strings, so it is a stock VASP build, as it should be for this check.

The test is resubmitted as 4484497, still one frame on 32 cores, and I'm waiting on it. If it runs cleanly, the 32-frame array goes in next. The README, INPROGRESS and restart record both the failure and the rerun.

The `load_intel` alias will break any other stock VASP job that uses `~/bin` binaries the same way. Your WSDA builds in `vasp.6.6.0/bin` evidently work with it.

### Claude (10-13 19:57)

The VASP test failed a second time (4484497), again in seconds, so it hasn't run any DFT yet. It's now resubmitted as 4485052.

There were two problems:
- **Intel environment:** sourcing the 2025.3 setvars didn't take effect in the batch job, so the MKL library was still missing.

In a completely clean environment (`env -i`) every library now resolves, so the job should start this time. The README, INPROGRESS and restart are updated.

Any other batch job that runs a stock `~/bin` VASP binary with `load_intel` will hit the same two problems.

### Claude (10-13 20:24)

The VASP test failed a fourth time (4485862), and I've resubmitted it as 4486053. Still no DFT has run.

- **What changed:** the libraries now load, but Intel MPI couldn't start because it found no network (libfabric) provider.
- **Cause:** the `srun` ranks don't inherit the oneAPI environment that setvars sets up in the batch shell, even though setvars itself works there.
- **Fix:** VASP now launches with Intel's own `mpirun -np $SLURM_NTASKS`, which passes the whole environment to every rank. Your working WSDA job templates launch the same way.
- **Diagnostic:** I cancelled the queued debug job (4485331), since the switch to `mpirun` makes it unnecessary.

The README, INPROGRESS and restart are updated with each failure. I'm watching 4486053 and will confirm the self-consistent loop is actually iterating before submitting the 32-frame array.

### Claude (10-13 20:47)

The VASP test passed: the first frame (bound pair, 140 GPa, 3000 K) finished in 7 minutes. The other 31 frames are now running as array 4487158.

| quantity | DFT | DeePMD | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| energy (eV) | −2602.06 | −2607.00 | +4.94 (9.7 meV/atom) |
| pressure, without the kinetic term (GPa) | 134.66 | 134.38 | +0.28 |
| forces | — | — | RMS error 0.07 eV/Å, on typical forces of 3.05 eV/Å |

- **Pressure (your EOS question):** at the same volume the model is within 0.3 GPa of DFT, about 0.2 %. So on this frame the EOS, and with it V at given P and T, is not where the gap to Ita & Cohen comes from.
- **Energy:** the 4.9 eV is an absolute offset and doesn't matter by itself. What counts for the vacancy energy is whether the bound-pair offset per atom matches the perfect-cell offset; that needs the perfect frames from the array.
- **Electronic entropy:** DFT's free energy and its energy without the entropy term differ by 0.84 eV here. I compare DeePMD with the free energy. That difference largely cancels between the perfect and bound-pair cells, but I'll check which of the two the training used.

Each frame takes about 7 minutes on 32 cores, so the array should finish within an hour or two of starting, queue permitting. Then `dft_compare.py` gives the DFT − DeePMD error in vacancy-pair formation energy at 20 and 140 GPa. The README, INPROGRESS and restart are updated.

### Claude (10-14 05:23)

The DFT spot check (part 1) is done. The model's equation of state is fine, but it puts the bound vacancy pair about 1 eV too low. Correcting for that closes part of the gap to Ita & Cohen, but they are still 1.4–2.6 eV higher.

VASP used Deng's training settings (PBEsol), on 8 MD snapshots each of the perfect and bound-pair MgO cells.

| | 20 GPa, 2000 K | 140 GPa, 3000 K |
|---|---|---|
| pressure error, DFT − DeePMD (GPa) | +0.01 / +0.07 | +0.21 / +0.27 |
| force RMSE (eV/Å) | 0.07–0.08 | 0.07 |
| ΔG_f model error, DFT − DeePMD | **+0.95 ± 0.08 eV** | **+1.27 ± 0.09 eV** |
| ΔG_f from TI (40 ps switching) | 5.15 ± 0.21 eV | 11.90 ± 0.24 eV |
| **DFT-corrected ΔG_f** | **6.10 ± 0.23 eV** | **13.17 ± 0.26 eV** (13.95 with 20 ps switching) |
| Ita & Cohen | 7.51 eV | 15.79 eV |

Pressure errors are given for the perfect / bound-pair cells.

- **EOS:** at the same volume DeePMD matches the DFT pressure to within 0.3 GPa in both cells. So V(P, T) and the P·ΔV term are not where the difference from Ita & Cohen comes from.
- **Model error:** the model puts the bound pair 1.0–1.3 eV too low. That is expected, since there are no defect configurations in its training set.
- **Electronic entropy:** the vacancy pair puts electronic states in the gap, so its cell has electronic entropy that the perfect cell doesn't. T·S_el is 0.17 eV at 2000 K and 0.80 eV at 3000 K. The correction above includes it; leaving it out would make the 140 GPa error 2.1 eV. Ita & Cohen's ionic model has no such term.
- **What's left (1.4–2.6 eV):** this is likely PBEsol DFT against their model potential, plus the formation-volume term in my free-energy integration, which hasn't converged. Part 2 would separate the two: static relaxed formation enthalpies from DFT and DeePMD, compared with published static DFT values.

**Next decision:** for the other states and the bridgmanite defects, we can either:
- apply this snapshot correction at each state (cheap, about 7 min of 32 cores per frame), or
- retrain the Deng model with vacancy configurations added.

I recommend per-state corrections for now, and retraining only if the corrections vary much between states.

Getting VASP to run took four failed test jobs. The stock `~/bin/vasp_gam` needs the older Intel oneAPI 2025.3 libraries plus HDF5 from `~/lib`, and has to be launched with Intel `mpirun`, not `srun`. `tools/vasp_array.sh` now does this, and I saved the recipe in memory.

Results are recorded in the `MgO_vacancy_DFTcheck` and A0 READMEs, INPROGRESS, DONE and the restart.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Frenkel–Ladd nonequilibrium TI:** ΔG_f = F_D − (N−L)/N F_I + P[V_D − (N−L)/N V_I].
   - **FEP from DeePMD to the DFT surface:**
     - dF_X = ⟨ΔE⟩ − var(ΔE)/(2kT);
     - δΔG_f = dF_D − (N−L)/N dF_I;
     - use Mermin TOTEN (it includes electronic entropy).
   - **Deng training DFT:** VASP PBEsol, 800 eV, SIGMA = kT, standard PAW Mg/O.
   - **Osetsky–Bacon two-block edge slab:**
     - v = (Lx/b)·d(Δx_top)/dt;
     - B = bτ/v;
     - η_eff = B/(ρb²);
     - τ_f = η_eff·γ̇;
     - ρ* = B/(η_max b²);
     - Granato–Lücke τ_d = BL²/(π²C), with C = μb²/2.
   - **VASP batch launch:**
     - oneAPI 2025.3 libraries plus ~/lib (HDF5);

atomic forces.
The related potential induced breathing
model was also used previously to study pressure effects
on excitons in alkali halides giving good agreement with
experiment and demonstrating that such models can give
good defect properties for ionic materials [14]. The VIB
model is a Gordon-Kim-type model [15] in which the total
charge density is modeled by overlapping ionic charge
densities which are computed using the local density
approximation (LDA) [16].
The total energy is a sum
of three terms: (a) the long-range electrostatic energy
computed using the Ewald method, (b) the self-energy of
each atom, and (c) the short-range interaction energy, the
sum of the kinetic, short-range electrostatic and exchange-
correlation energies from the LDA.
There are three
approximations beyond the LDA [17]: (i) The charge
density is modeled rather than computed self-consistently.
Comparisons with accurate linearized augmented plane
wave computations show this is a good approximation for
MgO [18].
(ii) The pair approximation is used for the
short-range interactions (c) which is a good approximation
as long as closed shell ions are used [19].
(iii) The
Thomas-Fermi kinetic energy is used for the short-range
overlap kinetic energy. The self-energy (b) includes the

**Tool `Bash`** — Compare lattice parameters with Tange 2009 MgO EOS

```
source ~/cohen_env/bin/activate; python - <<'EOF'
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.optimize import brentq
# Tange et al. 2009 JGR MgO, Vinet-MGD set (from memory; check): V0 per 4 f.u.
V0=74.698; K0=160.63; Kp=4.367; th0=761.; g0=1.442; aa=0.138; b=5.4
kB=1.380649e-23; n=8; N4=1 # 8 atoms per cell (4 MgO)
def gam(x): return g0*(1+aa*(x**b-1))
def theta(x):
    # integrate dln(theta) = -gamma dlnV
    f=lambda y: gam(y)/y
    return th0*np.exp(-quad(f,1,x)[0])
def Eth(T,th):
    D=lambda t: (3/t**3)*quad(lambda z: z**3/(np.exp(z)-1),0,t)[0]
    return 3*n*kB*T*D(th/T)
def P(V,T):
    x=V/V0; f=x**(1/3)
    Pv=3*K0*(1-f)/f**2*np.exp(1.5*(Kp-1)*(1-f))
    th=theta(x); g=gam(x)
    dPth=g/(V*1e-30)*(Eth(T,th)-Eth(300,th))/1e9
    return Pv+dPth
for Pt,T,ita,ours in [(20,2000,4.1312,16.6158943/4),(140,3000,3.7210,14.97706501/4)]:
    V=brentq(lambda V:P(V,T)-Pt,30,90); a=V**(1/3)
    print(Pt,T,'Tange a=%.4f  VIB %.4f (%.2f%%)  Deng/PBEsol %.4f (%.2f%%)'%(a,ita,100*(ita/a-1),ours,100*(ours/a-1)))
    # pressure of Tange at the other lattices
    print('   Tange P at VIB a: %.1f  at Deng a: %.1f GPa'%(P(ita**3,T),P(ours**3,T)))
EOF
```

### Claude (10-14 11:19)

Your VIB model (Ita & Cohen 1997) puts the bound vacancy pair 1–2.6 eV (about 6–19 %) higher than PBEsol DFT. Its equation of state is about as good as PBEsol's, so the difference is not coming from V(P, T). There is no direct DFT-vs-VIB calculation yet. The DFT side here is our Deng-model free energy plus the VASP snapshot correction.

**Lattice parameter at (P, T)**, against the Tange et al. 2009 experimental MgO thermal EOS. I took Tange's parameters from memory, so they need checking against the paper. The Deng model matches DFT pressure to within 0.3 GPa, so its lattice parameter stands in for PBEsol's.

| state | Tange a (Å) | VIB (Table I) | Deng / PBEsol |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 GPa, 2000 K | 4.1381 | 4.1312 (−0.17 %, Tange P = 21.0 GPa) | 4.1540 (+0.38 %, Tange P = 17.7 GPa) |
| 140 GPa, 3000 K | 3.7414 | 3.7210 (−0.55 %, Tange P = 149.9 GPa) | 3.7443 (+0.08 %, Tange P = 138.6 GPa) |

- Both are good. VIB is slightly too dense at high pressure (about +10 GPa), and PBEsol is slightly too expanded at 20 GPa.
- This volume difference changes the P·ΔV term by only about 0.1 eV, so it doesn't explain the ΔG_f gap.

**Bound-pair ΔG_f (eV)**

| state | DFT-corrected, with electronic entropy | DFT-corrected, without it | VIB | VIB − DFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 GPa, 2000 K | 6.10 ± 0.23 | 6.29 | 7.51 ± 0.25 | +1.2 to +1.4 |
| 140 GPa, 3000 K | 13.17–13.95 | 14.00–14.78 | 15.79 ± 0.69 | +1.0 to +2.6 |

The 140 GPa range comes from the two switching times (40 vs 20 ps), which differ through the formation-volume term.

- **Electronic entropy:** PBEsol's band gap (about 4.5–5 eV, against 7.8 eV measured) is too small. That overstates the in-gap vacancy states and their electronic entropy (T·S_el = 0.17 and 0.80 eV). The true value probably lies between the two DFT columns, nearer the column without electronic entropy at 3000 K.
- **At 140 GPa:** the difference is 1.5–3.5 times your ±0.69 eV error bar.
- **At 20 GPa:** the difference is about four times your ±0.25 eV error bar, so it is clearly significant.

**Likely causes, in my judgment:**
1. VIB's rigid, spherical, non-self-consistent ions can't redistribute charge around the vacancies or form in-gap states, which would make the defect too costly.
2. Our formation-volume term is still unconverged (0.8 eV spread at 140 GPa).
3. LDA vs PBEsol.

Part 2, static relaxed formation enthalpies from DFT and DeePMD, would separate these. Including VIB there needs a working VIB code. Do you still have one?

I've added both tables to the `MgO_vacancy_DFTcheck` README and summarised them in the A0 README.

```
#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Compare VASP single points with DeePMD on the same snapshots (tools/dft_snapshots_poscar.py layout).

Per frame directory (OUTCAR, dp.txt, dp_forces.txt):
    dE = E_DFT - E_DP   (E_DFT = 'free  energy   TOTEN', the energy DeePMD is trained on; also reports the
                         'energy  without entropy' value)                                                  (Eq. 1)
    dP = P_DFT - P_DP   (static pressure; VASP stress 'in kB' line, DeePMD virial only)                      (Eq. 2)
    force RMSE over all components.
Per state: mean and standard error of dE/N, dE and dP.
With --gf PERFECT DEFECT --L L: model error of the defect formation energy, as a free-energy perturbation from
the DeePMD to the DFT surface (second-order cumulant):
    dF_X = <dE>_X - var(dE)_X / (2 k_B T)                                                                  (Eq. 3)
    d(Delta G_f) = dF_D - (N-L)/N dF_I                                                                     (Eq. 4)
and the first-order version <dE>_D - (N-L)/N <dE>_I. Writes STATE/dft_compare.txt.
usage: dft_compare.py STATE [STATE ...] [--temp T]  |  dft_compare.py --gf PERFECT DEFECT --L 2 --temp T
"""
import argparse, glob, os, re
import numpy as np

KB = 8.617333262e-5

def outcar(fn):
    s = open(fn).read()
    if 'General timing and accounting' not in s:
        return None
    F = float(re.findall(r'free  energy   TOTEN\s+=\s+(\S+)', s)[-1])
    E0 = float(re.findall(r'energy  without entropy=\s+(\S+)', s)[-1])
    kb = [float(x) for x in re.findall(r'^\s+in kB(.*)$', s, re.M)[-1].split()]   # xx yy zz xy yz zx, kB
    blk = s.split('TOTAL-FORCE (eV/Angst)')[-1].split('\n')[2:]
    f = []
    for l in blk:
        if l.strip().startswith('---'):
            break
        f.append([float(x) for x in l.split()[3:6]])
    return F, E0, np.array(kb) * 0.1, np.array(f)                                # GPa

def state(sd):
    rows = []
    for fd in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(sd, 'f[0-9][0-9]'))):
        if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(fd, 'OUTCAR')):
            continue
        o = outcar(os.path.join(fd, 'OUTCAR'))
        if o is None:
            continue
        F, E0, s, f = o
        w = open(os.path.join(fd, 'dp.txt')).read().split(); d = dict(zip(w[::2], w[1::2]))
        fdp = np.loadtxt(os.path.join(fd, 'dp_forces.txt'))
        Pdft = s[:3].mean(); Pdp = float(d['P_bar']) / 1e4
        rows.append(dict(frame=os.path.basename(fd), N=int(d['N']), V=float(d['V'])

**Tool `Bash`** — Check MgO-only lattice at 175 GPa against Tange EOS

```
source ~/cohen_env/bin/activate; python - <<'EOF'
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.optimize import brentq
V0=74.698; K0=160.63; Kp=4.367; th0=761.; g0=1.442; aa=0.138; b=5.4; kB=1.380649e-23; n=8
gam=lambda x: g0*(1+aa*(x**b-1))
theta=lambda x: th0*np.exp(-quad(lambda y: gam(y)/y,1,x)[0])
def Eth(T,th): return 3*n*kB*T*(3/(th/T)**3)*quad(lambda z: z**3/np.expm1(z),0,th/T)[0]
def P(V,T):
    x=V/V0; f=x**(1/3); th=theta(x)
    return 3*K0*(1-f)/f**2*np.exp(1.5*(Kp-1)*(1-f))+gam(x)/(V*1e-30)*(Eth(T,th)-Eth(300,th))/1e9
print('edge 175/3500: Tange a=%.4f; Tange P at MgO-only a 3.7044: %.1f'%(brentq(lambda V:P(V,3500)-175,30,90)**(1/3),P(3.7044**3,3500)))
EOF
```

### Claude (10-14 11:37)

Your first MgO model (the MgO-only DeePMD model) has accurate forces but a pressure scale that runs high: 5–9 GPa above PBEsol DFT at the same volume, and 7–13 GPa above the experimental EOS. I ran it on the same 32 configurations as the VASP spot check, so no new DFT jobs were needed. The full write-up, with a two-panel figure (PDF and PNG), is `results_dft/MGO_DFT_MODEL_COMPARISON.md`; I also added a summary section 5l.

The tables compare against PBEsol DFT (the Deng training settings), the Deng model, Ita & Cohen's VIB model, and the experimental MgO EOS of Tange et al. 2009. I quoted the Tange parameters from memory, so they still need checking against the paper.

**Pressure scale (equation of state)**

| | 20 GPa, 2000 K | 140 GPa, 3000 K | 175 GPa, 3500 K |
|---|---|---|---|
| PBEsol DFT − MgO-only model, same volume | −4.9 GPa | −9.2 GPa | – |
| MgO-only model − experiment (Tange) | +7.2 GPa | +10.6 GPa | +12.5 GPa |
| Deng model (≈ PBEsol) − experiment | +2.3 GPa | +1.4 GPa | – |
| VIB − experiment | −1.0 GPa | −9.9 GPa | – |

- The MgO-only error grows with compression, which points to a different functional rather than a fitting error. My guess is PBE, but the graph file only stores training-set names, not the DFT settings. **Can you confirm what functional and settings it was trained with?**
- VIB and the MgO-only model miss experiment by similar amounts in opposite directions. PBEsol is the closest.

**Forces and vacancy energetics**

- **Forces:** against PBEsol, the MgO-only model's force error is 0.054–0.074 eV/Å. That matches or beats the Deng model (0.066–0.082 eV/Å), and is 2–4 % of the RMS force.
- **Bound vacancy pair:** the MgO-only model puts the pair too low by +0.72 ± 0.08 eV at 20 GPa and +0.96 ± 0.08 eV at 140 GPa. The Deng model is too low by +0.95 and +1.27 eV.
  - Neither model saw vacancies in training.
  - Part of the MgO-only difference may come from PBE vs PBEsol rather than the model itself. A PBE rerun of a few frames would separate the two, once I know the training settings.
- **VIB:** its pair formation free energies are 1.0–2.6 eV (6–19 %) above the DFT-corrected values (6.10 and 13.2–14.8 eV, against 7.51 and 15.79). The EOS difference accounts for 0.1 eV or less of that.

**What this changes in earlier results:** every pressure we've quoted for MgO-only runs is about 7–13 GPa too high on the experimental scale.
- The V6.6868 runs, quoted as 175–193 GPa, are really about 162–180 GPa.
- The edge-dislocation run labelled 175 GPa is at about 162 GPa. That is still inside Perez's 175 ± 15 GPa, so that comparison stands.
- Results compared at fixed volume are unaffected.
- The MgO-vs-MgSiO₃ comparison at V = 6.5669 mixes two models, so its quoted pressures carry a 5–9 GPa offset between the minerals.

I haven't relabelled the summary pressures yet. I'd like to measure the offset directly at the V6.6868 and V9.6397 states first.

**Tools and records:**
- New `tools/dp_rescore.py` scores the DFT frames with any DeePMD model. As a check, scoring with the Deng model reproduced the original MD energies and pressures exactly.
- `dft_compare.py` has a new `--tag` option that compares against those scores.
- New `tools/plot_dft_model_comparison.py` makes the figure.
- Records are updated in the DFT README, INPROGRESS, DONE, the restart file and memory.

  Static (NEB) barriers at the same volume, the next step, will separate these effects.
- **Consequence for extrapolation:** an activation energy fitted at high T underestimates relaxation times at lower T. Here it would be off by a factor of about 3 already at 3500 K, for oxygen.

### Claude (10-15 06:51)

Yes, kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) fits that window well, but only for some mechanisms. My recommendation is a quick vacancy KMC first to validate the method, then point KMC at grain boundaries and dislocations, which are the realistic seismic candidates.

**How the anelastic spectrum would come out.** Our NEMD stops near GHz because the trajectory is ns long. KMC jumps from one atomic event to the next, so its time step is the inverse of the total event rate, not a vibration period.
- No driving is needed. Run equilibrium KMC, record the defect elastic dipoles G(t) (our §5c tensors) and use fluctuation–dissipation:
  ΔM(t) = ⟨δ(ΣG:E)(0) · δ(ΣG:E)(t)⟩ / (V k_B T),
  which is the time-dependent form of Eq. 11. Its Fourier transform gives M″(ω) from 1/t_KMC up to the hop rate, often 1 Hz to GHz in one run.
- Driven KMC also works: §5b already has the strain derivatives of the barriers (dE_b/dε ≈ 10–19 eV), so applied stress can tilt the rates directly.
- The GHz overlap with NEMD and MD gives a built-in check. Harmonic transition-state theory already matches the MD Mg hop rates within 1.0–1.5× with no fitting.

**Where the frequencies land.** Rates from our NEB barriers and prefactors at the V6.6868 volume, which is static 116 GPa:

| T | bound-pair rotation, Mg | rotation, O | isolated O vacancy | barrier needed for a 1 Hz peak |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 K | 1×10⁷ s⁻¹ | 8×10⁵ | 40 | 5.3 eV |
| 2500 K | 3×10⁸ | 3×10⁷ | 1×10⁴ | 6.6 eV |
| 3000 K | 2×10⁹ | 3×10⁸ | 4×10⁵ | 7.9 eV |

So single vacancy events at mantle temperatures sit at kHz–GHz. The seismic band needs effective barriers of about 6–8 eV, which means collective or cooperative processes.

**What KMC would and wouldn't add:**
1. **Isolated and bound Schottky pairs.** A master equation gives a single Debye peak exactly, and §5c already shows its strength is negligible (Q⁻¹ ≈ 5×10⁻⁵). KMC adds value only through interactions: clustering, a spread of local environments, and the missing O mechanisms (MD O hops are 2–3× faster than our event list predicts). Any of these could broaden the peak into an absorption band. This is cheap, about days of work, because the event list and dipoles already exist. It is a good method validator but probably won't change the seismic conclusion.
2. **Grain boundaries.** At 20 GPa the boundary slides freely at THz. KMC driven by the DeePMD model, finding events on the fly, could follow it to µs–s.
   - The low-barrier "flicker" problem is serious at a boundary, so this needs basin acceleration.
   - At 140 GPa the boundary events are 14–30 eV collective steps, which KMC can't sample without first finding them.
   - The output would be boundary viscosity and diffusivity to feed a grain-scale model (Raj–Ashby / Morris–Jackson). A millimetre grain can't be simulated atom by atom.
3. **Dislocations: my pick for the seismic question.** Our edge run (§5k) shows drag is far too fast for seismic loss, and that the dislocation stops gliding below τ ≈ 0.25–0.5 GPa.
   - A line-level KMC can model a pinned segment that moves by thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and unpinning from vacancies.
   - It would take its barriers from NEB, its mobility (B) from our runs, and its pinning energies from vacancy–dislocation binding.
   - It is the standard route to thermally activated Granato–Lücke loss and could put a peak in the 0.01–1 Hz band.

"Faster than diffusion" comes out naturally. Local hops give a bounded (anelastic) relaxation. If sinks such as boundaries or dislocations are included, KMC also shows the crossover to steady diffusional creep at low ω, so it can mark where anelasticity ends and viscous flow begins.

**Proposed order:**
1. Vacancy KMC in MgO with the existing NEB event list plus dipoles, run at 2000–4000 K and validated against the MD rates and NEMD.
2. Kink-pair and pinning barriers for the ½⟨110⟩{001} edge, then a dislocation-line KMC.
3. Boundary KMC at 20 GPa.

Do you want me to write this up as a plan with costs, or start step 1?

The PBE comparison job (4520046) is still waiting in the queue. I'll analyse it when it finishes.

## 5d. Grain-boundary sliding from equilibrium MD, and a grain-scale model (T18 steps 1 and 3)

- **Runs:** Σ5 bicrystal, 20 ps NVT + 300 ps NVE, no applied strain (job 4264732; `MgO/4096atoms/GBslide`; `tools/gb_slide.py`; `results/fig_gb_sliding`).
- **Friction from diffusion:** the relative displacement $u$ of the two grain interiors diffuses with

$$D_u=\frac{k_BT}{2\beta A},\qquad \eta_{cell}=\frac{\beta L_z}{2} \tag{12}$$

  for friction β per boundary (stress = β × sliding velocity) and boundary area $A=L_xL_y$.

#   types 1,2 mobile Mg,O; 3,4 bottom rigid (fixed); 5,6 top rigid (moves as a block under the applied forces).
# Plan: Anelasticity/ANELASTICITY_PLAN_FE_DISLOCATIONS.md §3a (Eqs. 11-12). Analysis: tools/disl_velocity.py.
# Stages: minimize (blocks fixed) -> TEQ steps at TEMP with the piston only -> for each TAU (GPa): TRUN steps.
# Output: drive.dat  step  tau(GPa)  dx_top(Å)  dy_top(Å)  T_mobile(K)  pe  sxx syy szz sxy (GPa, mobile region)
# -var DATA MODEL TEMP PRESS(GPa) TAU 0.1 0.25 0.5 1.0 (index variable: one run per value, in order) [TEQ 10000] [TRUN 30000] [SEED 777] [TMAP "Mg O Mg O Mg O"]
#      [TIMEOUT 86100]
variable        TEQ index 10000
variable        TRUN index 30000
variable        SEED index 777
variable        TMAP index "Mg O Mg O Mg O"
variable        TIMEOUT index 86100
timer           timeout ${TIMEOUT} every 1000
units           metal
atom_style      atomic
boundary        p f p
atom_modify     map array
read_data       ${DATA}
pair_style      deepmd ${MODEL}
variable        syy equal -c_ss[2]/v_vmob/1e4
variable        szz equal -c_ss[3]/v_vmob/1e4
variable        sxy equal -c_ss[4]/v_vmob/1e4
thermo          1000
thermo_style    custom step v_tau v_dx v_dy c_tmob pe v_sxx v_syy v_szz v_sxy
fix             pr all print 100 "$(step) $(v_tau:%.3f) $(v_dx:%.4f) $(v_dy:%.4f) $(c_tmob:%.1f) $(pe:%.4f) $(v_sxx:%.3f) $(v_syy:%.3f) $(v_szz:%.3f) $(v_sxy:%.3f)" file drive.dat screen no title "# step tau_GPa dx_top_A dy_top_A T_mob pe sxx syy szz sxy (GPa; stress/atom with an approximate mobile volume; compressive positive)"
run             ${TEQ}
write_data      eq_piston.data nocoeff

label           tloop
variable        tau equal ${TAU}
print           "TAU_START ${TAU} GPa at step $(step)"
run             ${TRUN}
write_data      state_tau${TAU}.data nocoeff
print           "TAU_DONE ${TAU} dx_top $(v_dx:%.4f) A"
next            TAU
jump            SELF tloop
print           "DRIVE_DONE"
```

### Claude (10-15 07:10)

Driving to make the collective events happen, then focusing on dislocations and grain boundaries, is now the plan in `ANELASTICITY_PLAN_DRIVEN_RHEOLOGY.md`. The first dislocation runs are in the queue. The plan:

1. **Drive** with stress, strain rate or large-amplitude oscillation, so kink pairs, unpinning and boundary steps happen within MD time. MD finds the mechanism and its rate at high stress.
2. **Anchor at low stress.** NEB (and PLUMED biasing along the driven coordinate) on the path MD found, at zero and intermediate stress, gives the barrier as a function of stress.
3. **Rate law.** A standard stress-dependent barrier form (Eq. 1) then gives the linear-response mobility at seismic stress amplitudes (≲ 1 MPa), which no driven run can measure directly (Eq. 3).
4. **Mesoscale models:**
   - dislocations: a Granato–Lücke line model with thermally activated glide and pinning;
   - boundaries: a grain-size model (Eq. 4) combining elastically accommodated sliding (relaxation time ∝ d) with diffusional creep (∝ d³). A spread of boundary types turns the single peak into an absorption band.
   - Both give Q⁻¹(ω, T, P, d) in the seismic band.
5. **Validate** where driven MD, the rate law and the GHz sweeps overlap.

**Main risk:** the mechanism found at GPa stresses may not be the one that operates at MPa. I'll step the stress down until events stop and check that the path and activation volume stay the same. For boundaries I'll use pre-existing disconnections rather than nucleation, because a nucleation barrier diverges as stress goes to zero.

**This changes the grain-boundary approach.** The 3×1 boundary NEB (4407041) finished. Its barrier is 28.3 eV (0.17 J/m² per boundary, not fully converged), and the saddle displacement is spread evenly across the whole 89 Å boundary. So the 140 GPa Σ5 boundary moves only by collective steps; no local step forms on its own. Low-stress boundary kinetics will therefore have to come from disconnections built in explicitly (step G1), which I'll build next.

**Running now:** step D1, 4 GPU jobs of about 10 h each (4593708–4593711).
- Edge dislocation in MgO at 175 GPa / 3500 K, with the line 4× longer than before (about 33,000 atoms) so kink pairs fit.
- Constant stress of 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 and 0.5 GPa, 150 ps each. That brackets the 0.25–0.5 GPa threshold where glide stopped in the short-line run.
- I added an optional trajectory dump to the dislocation scripts, so I can track the dislocation core and tell jerky kink-pair motion from smooth glide.

**Before submitting, I'll check with you on the two large items** (about 150 GPU-hours each):
- G4: other boundary types plus a small polycrystal with triple junctions, needed so the grain-size model isn't based on Σ5 alone;
- D7: dislocations in bridgmanite.

# Bridgmanite (MgSiO₃) Rheology — Literature Map

Oct 12, 2026 · @Ron

Direct high-T bridgmanite deformation data exist only up to \~27 GPa and down to \~10⁻⁶ s⁻¹; theory (mostly the Lille group) fills in the rest. The two camps now disagree on what deforms the mantle: dislocation creep, diffusion creep, or diffusion-controlled pure climb.

## Overview — where the field stands

- **Mechanism at mantle conditions.** Dislocation creep: Tsujino et al. 2022, Guan et al. 2026. Diffusion creep: Karato et al. 1995, Ammann et al. 2010. Pure climb creep: Boioli et al. 2017, Reali et al. 2019, Cordier et al. 2023.
- **Dominant slip system.** 001 at 25 GPa, 1873 K (Tsujino 2016); T-switch 010 → 100 near 1800 K (Guan 2026); P-switch (100) → (010) between 24 and 50 GPa (Gay 2024; theory: Hirel 2014, Kraych 2016).
- **Bdg vs Fp in aggregates.** Fp-weak, strain-localizing (Girard 2016, Nzogang 2018) vs Bdg load-bearing (Xu F. 2022, Cordier 2023).
- **Grain size and the \~1000 km viscosity jump.** Grain-size driven (Fei 2023) vs grain-size-insensitive dislocation creep (Guan 2026) vs fabric-driven seismic discontinuity (Magali 2026).
- **Gap.** No high-T flow-law data above \~30 GPa; Al, Fe³⁺ and water effects on creep are barely measured.

A five-paper entry path: Tsujino 2022 (flow law), Kraych 2016 (glide theory), Boioli 2017 (climb creep), Fei 2023 (grain size), Guan 2026 (slip transition). Entries marked † were cited from memory and not opened; check them before citing.

## Experiments — strength and flow stress

Direct bridgmanite strength data span room-T DAC (radial XRD) to \~2100 K in multi-anvil/RDA; all are at strain rates \~10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, so every number here needs extrapolation by \~10 orders of magnitude to mantle rates.

### Claude (10-15 08:49)

I'm still waiting on two of the three paper reviews: the van Driel thesis and Fei 2023 / Ritterbex 2020. The review of the MgO grain-boundary and dislocation papers is back, and it raises two problems with our current runs.

1. **The dislocation line is too short to show kink pairs.** Cordier 2012 gives a critical kink-pair width of 60–80 b for the ½⟨110⟩{100} edge, which is about 150–200 Å at 175 GPa and wider at low stress. Our new 64 Å line is shorter than that.
   - So the "no glide below 0.25 GPa" threshold and the four runs now going (4593708–11) depend on line length and don't measure kink-pair kinetics. They are still useful for drag and the onset of glide.
   - Real kink-pair runs need lines of at least 300–400 Å. A thinner slab at about 60,000 atoms is my first guess; I'll size it after these finish.
   - By the review's estimate, our 0.25–0.5 GPa onset is about 2× below Cordier's extrapolated prediction (0.6–1.1 GPa). That is within the uncertainty, but not yet a real test.
2. **Our Σ5 grain boundary probably migrates in a different mode from van Driel 2020's.** Our coupling of about 0.6 is the ⟨100⟩ mode (theory 0.667), while theirs is 1.0, the ⟨110⟩ mode. Their barrier and critical stress therefore don't apply directly to our 20 GPa sliding.
   - What does line up: they find structural transitions of this boundary near 6 GPa and 90–100 GPa. Their high-pressure barriers (0.20–0.26 J/m² at 100–122 GPa) extrapolate to about 0.3 J/m² at 140 GPa, in line with our 0.17–0.5 J/m². That fits our "slides at 20 GPa, locked at 140 GPa".
   - I'll check whether our reconstructed 140 GPa boundary is their high-pressure structure (a half-period offset along the tilt axis).

When the other two reviews arrive I'll write a single comparison note and fold these changes into the plan.

### Claude (10-15 08:51)

I've read the papers. The main lesson is that clean grain boundaries slide too easily to cause seismic attenuation, so the plan now centres on what blocks and accommodates sliding: triple junctions and boundary diffusion. The full notes, with numbers and comparisons, are in `LITERATURE_NOTES_2026-10-15.md`, and the revisions are in plan §5.

**Grain boundaries (van Driel 2020 and thesis).**
- **Same boundary as ours.** Their twin is our Σ5 (310)/[001] boundary, computed with static PBE DFT. Its structure changes at about 5 GPa and again at about 90–100 GPa, and the migration barrier jumps with each change: about 50 mJ/m² (critical stress about 1.5 GPa) in the middle range, then 0.20–0.26 J/m² (8–12 GPa) above 100 GPa.
- **Agreement:** that matches our "slides at 20 GPa, locked at 140 GPa". Their high-pressure barrier extrapolates to about 0.3 J/m² at 140 GPa, inside our 0.17–0.5 J/m².
- **Difference:** they impose a coupling factor of 1.0 (the ⟨110⟩ mode), while our MD picks about 0.6 (the ⟨100⟩ mode). Their barriers may belong to a different mechanism.
- **Their gap:** they assume a whole grain face moves at once, so the barrier scales with grain size squared. That is exactly what the explicit disconnections in our plan address.
- **Bridgmanite:** they made a GAP potential for bridgmanite and studied six [100] tilt boundaries, with energies, structures and boundary diffusion of Mg, Si and O.
  - Their Coble creep matches lower-mantle viscosity for grain sizes of 5 mm–4 cm.
  - They ran no driven MD, no sliding friction and no attenuation, so our approach adds something new there.

**Dislocations (Cordier, Amodeo & Carrez 2012; Carrez 2009; Ferré 2007).**
- Cordier 2012 gives Peierls stresses and kink-pair energies for MgO up to 100 GPa. Extrapolated to 175 GPa, they predict an MD onset near 0.6–1.1 GPa, against our 0.25–0.5 GPa: the same order.
- **Our dislocation lines are too short.** The critical kink-pair width is about 150–200 Å, and our running lines are 64 Å. Those runs will give drag and the glide onset, not kink pairs. Kink-pair runs need lines of at least 300 Å (about 60,000 atoms), plus screw dislocations.
- The simpler 1D model (Carrez 2009) overestimates the friction of this edge by about 12×.
- Bridgmanite's lattice friction is about 10× MgO's.

**Grain size (Fei et al. 2023; Ritterbex 2020).**
- Fei's lower-mantle grain sizes are about 0.3–1 mm for pyrolite and 1–5 mm for bridgmanite-rich rock. Their viscosity jump rests on Si lattice diffusion with an activation volume borrowed from olivine.
- Our planned Ita & Cohen-style vacancy free energies for Si in bridgmanite would test that directly.
- Some of Fei's printed formulas don't check out: the climb-creep equation is dimensionally inconsistent and the growth-rate fit signs look wrong.

**What this changes in the plan.**
- **Clean-boundary sliding is too fast.** Our Σ5 friction at 20 GPa relaxes in 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁷ s for 0.3–5 mm grains. That lowers the modulus but gives no seismic-band loss. Pure diffusional relaxation, at the other extreme, takes about 10¹² s.
- **The seismic band lies in between,** and depends on how sliding is blocked (triple junctions, steps) and accommodated (boundary diffusion). So the polycrystal with triple junctions and the boundary diffusion coefficients become central, not extras.
- **New cheap static checks:**
  - D0: DeePMD stacking-fault energies, elastic constants and the 0 K Peierls stress against Carrez and Cordier;
  - G0: Σ5 boundary energies and structures against van Driel's table, including whether our 140 GPa reconstruction is his high-pressure structure, plus barriers for both coupling modes.
- I renamed our boundary friction from β to ζ_GB, because β is also the coupling factor.

**Decisions for you:**
1. **Bridgmanite boundaries:** shall I start from van Driel's [100] tilt boundaries, (021) first, then (013) and (011)? You'd asked me to wait for your literature review.
2. **Large runs, roughly 150 GPU-hours each:** the long-line kink-pair runs and the polycrystal. Should I submit them once D0 and G0 are done?

Next I'll start the D0 and G0 static checks, which are cheap. Records are updated: plan §5, DONE and the restart file.

The four dislocation runs are about 2 h into their roughly 9 h. The PBE check (4520046) is still waiting in the queue.

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Boundary profiles z_b(x) of a z-normal <001>-tilt bicrystal from a per-atom grain-orientation order parameter.

Each atom gets the mean angle (mod 90 deg) of its in-plane (xz) nearest-neighbour bonds; atoms closer to the
orientation of grain A (median at z in --za) than to grain B (--zb) count as A. In each of NX slices along x the
A fraction is profiled along z, and the two crossings (B->A and A->B) are the boundary heights. A localized step
(disconnection) shows up as a jump of z_b between slices; uniform motion of the whole plane does not.

usage: gb_orient.py RUN FRAME0 FRAME1 [--nx 6] [--za 10 20] [--zb 40 50]       (MD snapshots, RUN/snap.dump)
       gb_orient.py RUN/quench_I_J.traj 0 N [...]                               (quenched structures, ASE traj)
       gb_orient.py RUN/quench F0 F1 [...]                         (LAMMPS quenches: quench_<f>.data, quench.dat)
"""
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

def orient(p, L):
    q = p % L; t = cKDTree(q, boxsize=L)
    _, j = t.query(q, k=7)
    v = q[j[:, 1:]] - q[:, None, :]; v -= L * np.round(v / L)
    phi = np.radians(np.degrees(np.arctan2(v[..., 2], v[..., 0])) % 90)
    keep = np.abs(v[..., 1]) < 0.8                                   # in-plane bonds only
    c = np.where(keep, np.cos(4 * phi), 0).sum(1); s = np.where(keep, np.sin(4 * phi), 0).sum(1)

- Guan et al., Commun. Earth Environ. 7, 183 (2026): `s43247-026-03212-9.pdf` and its SI.
- Perez et al., PRB 111, 144108 (2025): `Perez.pdf`.

## 0. Why this matters, and what the papers set up

- **Cordier et al. 2023.**
  - Claim: periclase deforms 10³–10⁷× more slowly than bridgmanite at mantle strain rates, so the lower mantle's rheology is that of bridgmanite.
  - Basis: climb in MgO is limited by O self-diffusion, which they take from the **Ita & Cohen fit** (their Eq. 1, Table 1). D_O falls to 10⁻³¹ m²/s at 90–120 GPa.
  - Bridgmanite side: pure climb creep (Reali et al. 2019) with an assumed vacancy fraction $X_v=10^{-5}$.
  - The conclusion therefore rests on (i) D_O(P,T) in MgO and (ii) diffusion in bridgmanite. Both are what an Ita–Cohen-type calculation gives, and DeePMD can now do it for both minerals with the same model.
  - *Note:* Cordier Table 1 lists $E_0=0.4\times10^{-19}$ J. Their Table 2 enthalpies (9.15 eV at 30 GPa, 15.09 eV at 120 GPa) are reproduced only with Ita & Cohen's $E_0\approx9.4\times10^{-19}$ J (5.9 eV) for O. The 0.4 appears to be a typo; only Table 1 is affected.
- **Guan et al. 2026** (25 GPa, 1700–2100 K, strain rates 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁴ s⁻¹):
  - The dominant slip system changes at about 1800 K, from [010](100) below to [100](010) above.
  - The authors argue that dislocation creep, not diffusion or pure climb creep, may control the lower mantle.
  - The mechanism of the change is unknown. A temperature-dependent crossover of the lattice friction (Peierls stress) or mobility of the two systems is the obvious candidate, and MD can test it directly.
- **Perez et al. 2025** (laser-driven Richtmyer–Meshkov):
  - Solid single-crystal MgO has an effective viscosity of at most about $10^2$ Pa s at 175 ± 15 GPa, about 3500 K and $\dot\varepsilon=10^6$–$10^7$ s⁻¹. That implies a flow stress of about 1 GPa or less.
  - The conditions are close to our V6.6868 MgO crystal (140–190 GPa).
  - In the athermal glide regime, a drag-controlled dislocation population has the Newtonian effective viscosity of Eq. 12 below. MD can compute the drag coefficient $B$ at these conditions.
- **Correction to our own records (summary §5c, and the bridgmanite "≈ 1.9 eV per pair" note in `crystal_VMgO/README.md`).**
  - The fixed-V quantity $E(N-2)-\frac{N-2}{N}E_{perf}$ (2.44 eV in MgO) leaves out the $P\,v_f$ term of Eq. 3 below. At 140–190 GPa that term is of order $P\cdot2\Omega\approx$ 12–16 eV.

similar to those presented in several later theoretical studies18–20.
Modelling dislocation creep of periclase
To model plasticity of periclase under mantle conditions we use a 2.5D 
DD simulation approach already benchmarked for periclase at ambient 
pressure11. DD simulation is a modelling tool that describes the collec-
tive motion and interactions of dislocations at the mesoscale. This 
technique is based on continuum elasticity theory, which provides the 
description of the elastic field induced by dislocations in a crystal, their 
interactions with each other and with respect to the stress field result-
ing from external loading. Within our DD code, dislocation glide is 
coupled with climb to investigate high-temperature creep (Methods). 
Our creep results are presented in Fig. 2a, which shows the creep strain 
rates obtained from the 2.5D DD simulations as a function of the creep 
stress for the four (P, T) conditions selected. A constant slope is found 
for all these strain rate–stress curves, which gives the value of the power 
law stress exponent, n = 3.1. A strong pressure dependence is found 
between (30 GPa, 2,000 K) and (90 GPa, 2,500 K), whereas creep rates 
at (90 GPa, 2,500 K) and (120 GPa, 2,800 K) are very close due to very 
similar values for the diffusion coefficients (Fig. 1 and Table 2). On 
Fig. 2a we compare the creep rates of periclase with those of bridgman-
ite at the same depths. For bridgmanite, we use the results of Reali 
et al.21 for pure climb creep (PCC) with a vacancy concentration 
Xv = 1 × 10−5; these results were shown to be in good agreement with 
empirical geophysical constraints on the viscosity profile of Earth’s 
lower mantle. Bridgmanite and periclase exhibit similar stress expo-
nents. However, we see that these calculations lead to bridgmanite 
having higher creep rates than periclase at any depth. To better illus-

### Claude (10-15 09:52)

You're welcome! Both comparisons are written up. The main result is that Cordier et al.'s "periclase deforms more slowly than bridgmanite" holds deep in the lower mantle but is no longer secure near 800 km, and a fast grain-boundary path in periclase could reverse it everywhere.

**Cordier et al. 2023 (the paper you meant):** `results_cordier2023/CORDIER2023_COMPARISON.md`
- **Their diffusion law is your fit.** Their O diffusion in MgO is the Ita & Cohen expression. The E₀ printed in their Table 1 (0.4×10⁻¹⁹ J) is a typo for 9.4×10⁻¹⁹ J; with that value their Eq. 1 reproduces their Table 2 to 2 %.
- **The DFT correction speeds O diffusion.** Our DFT check puts the vacancy-pair formation free energy 1–2.6 eV below the VIB value. That makes O diffusion faster by about ×8–1900 along their geotherm (assuming the free vacancy pair carries a similar error, which is not yet checked).
  - Their periclase/bridgmanite viscosity contrast (10³–10⁷) drops by 1–3 orders.
  - Near 800 km, "periclase slower" is no longer secure: about 0.5–60 instead of 10³.
  - Their own FeO estimate (×2000) points the same way.
- **The biggest lever is one they leave out.** Cordier ignore grain boundaries. With the boundary O diffusion we measured in our MgO Σ5 boundary (an upper bound, measured at lower pressure), Coble creep would make fine-grained periclase about 10⁷ times faster than their lattice-diffusion value. That would reverse the conclusion.
  - The decisive unknown is boundary O diffusion in MgO at 30–120 GPa. That is a cheap calculation, and I've made it the top new item.
- **The comparison is asymmetric.** Bridgmanite uses an assumed vacancy fraction (10⁻⁵), while periclase is intrinsic. Our planned bridgmanite vacancy free energies, with the same model as MgO, give the first intrinsic-to-intrinsic comparison.
- **Glide assumption.** They assume athermal, drag-limited glide in MgO. Our edge-dislocation drag (B = 2.2×10⁻⁴ Pa s) tests their B ∝ T scaling at one condition. The long-line runs will test whether glide is really athermal at depth; if it isn't, their conclusion gets stronger there.

**Fei et al. 2023:** `results_fei2023/FEI2023_COMPARISON.md`, with `tools/fei2023_model.py`
- I re-implemented their model and it reproduces their Fig. 4a–c, with one fix: their printed climb-creep equation is dimensionally wrong, and the correct (Nabarro) form needs a factor of 3.3 to match their figure.
- Their growth-rate fit coefficients appear with inverted signs in the text.
- Putting periclase into their framework, the MgO/MgSiO₃ viscosity ratio spans about 10⁷ depending on how O moves in periclase: intrinsic lattice, extrinsic, or along boundaries.

**Running:**
- **Long-line dislocation runs** (262 Å line, 4602367/68): queued. They are untested at about 68,000 atoms, so they may run out of GPU memory.
- **Short-line runs** (4593708–11): running.

- **PBE check** (4520046): still queued.

### Claude (10-15 09:54)

The MgO polycrystal builder is done: `tools/build_mgo_polycrystal.py`. It has only been checked geometrically so far; no LAMMPS has run on its output.

- **What it builds:** a periodic Voronoi polycrystal of MgO with randomly oriented grains and exact Mg:O stoichiometry. It also writes which grain each atom belongs to, plus the grain orientations and misorientations, for grain-resolved diffusion and rotation analysis. It can write either the MgO-only model's atom types or the Deng model's.
- **Test builds:** about 26,500 atoms with 8 grains of about 3.7 nm at the 27 GPa lattice, and about 24,500 atoms with 8 grains of about 3.4 nm at the 120 GPa lattice. All boundaries are high-angle (19–59°), and about 19 % of atoms sit in boundaries.
- **Limits:** the grains are small, every grain touches every other one, and there are no special or low-angle boundaries.
- **Before use:** the as-built boundaries need a long anneal (≥ 100 ps NPT at high temperature) before any diffusion or driven run.
- **Next:** anneal the polycrystals with the Deng model at Cordier's geotherm states, the same model as for bridgmanite.

The bridgmanite tilt-boundary builder is still in progress. The PBE check (4520046) is still queued.

### Claude (10-15 09:56)

Both structure builders are finished, but neither has been relaxed or run in LAMMPS yet. The bridgmanite builder and the comparison write-ups are new since my last update.

**Bridgmanite tilt-boundary builder** (`tools/build_bdg_tilt_gb.py`)
- **What it builds:** symmetric [100]-tilt boundaries in bridgmanite on van Driel's planes, two boundaries per periodic cell. It can also generate a set of rigidly shifted versions, so the lowest-energy boundary structure can be found after relaxation.
- **Tests:** (021) at 6,560 atoms, (013) at 6,960 and (011) at 7,470, all with about 3 nm grains.
  - Stoichiometry is exact, and the grain interiors match bulk bridgmanite.
  - Atoms across the boundaries come as close as 1.46–1.58 Å, so each structure needs relaxing before use.
- **Lattice input:** the atomic positions are ambient-pressure values in a cell compressed to about 25 GPa. Production cells will take the lattice from the Deng model at each pressure and temperature.

**MgO polycrystal builder** (`tools/build_mgo_polycrystal.py`)
- **Tests:** about 26,000 atoms, 8 randomly oriented grains of about 3.7 nm; about 19 % of atoms are in boundaries.

**Comparison write-ups**

- **Fei et al. 2023:** `results_fei2023/FEI2023_COMPARISON.md`.

### Claude (10-15 10:52)

The OCTP comparison was finished on 2026-10-09. OCTP works and agrees with our Green–Kubo analysis, but it gives us nothing new.

- **How it's installed:** OCTP (Jamali et al. 2019) is built as a LAMMPS plugin and loaded at run time with `plugin load` (`build_octp_plugin/octpplugin.so`). The production LAMMPS was not changed.
- **Test:** a 120 ps constant-energy run of the 8000 K MgO liquid (job 4236292). I compared OCTP's Einstein-form viscosity with the Green–Kubo running integral from the same trajectory.
  - **Agreement:** they match from 2 fs to 2 ps. OCTP's plateau of about 8.2 mPa s (0.2–2 ps) matches η₀ = 8.19 mPa s from the 1.5 ns Green–Kubo run.
  - **Cost:** none; it ran at 23.8 steps/s with or without OCTP.
  - **Long lags:** beyond about 3 ps both are dominated by noise. That is expected, because the two forms are mathematically equivalent.
  - **Bias:** OCTP's running estimate converges more slowly and lies low at short times.
- **What it's good for:** `fix ordern` samples the correlation functions efficiently, so it can run alongside other measurements and saves storing the stress series. It is not a multiple-time-step integrator, so it doesn't reach longer times or lower frequencies.
- **Longer times:** r-RESPA (multiple time steps) isn't supported by the DeePMD pair style. That is why we've moved to driven runs and barrier-based rates for the slow processes.

The write-up is in results summary §5 and the figure is `results/fig_octp_vs_gk.{pdf,png}`. The open-items list at the end of the summary still listed OCTP as pending, so I marked it done.

Build periodic symmetric [100]-tilt grain-boundary bicrystals of MgSiO3 bridgmanite (Pbnm) for LAMMPS.

Follows van Driel (PhD thesis, UCL 2021, ch. 6): symmetric tilt boundaries about [100] on (0kl) = (021), (013),
(011), and optionally (012), (014), (023). Output: LAMMPS data, atom_style atomic, types 1 Mg, 2 Si, 3 O
(Deng DeePMD model order), orthogonal box, optional Maxwell velocities.

Unit cell. Generated from lattice parameters plus Wyckoff positions in Pbnm (No. 62, setting cab; Si on the
inversion centres 4b). Defaults are approximate values at about 25 GPa and 300 K:
    a, b, c = 4.634, 4.813, 6.692 Å  (V = 149.25 Å^3, Z = 4). These come from a third-order Birch-Murnaghan EOS
    (V0 = 162.3 Å^3, K0 = 253 GPa, K0' = 4) with axial ratios close to the measured ones at that pressure;
    Mg 4c (0.5141, 0.5560, 1/4), Si 4b (1/2, 0, 0), O1 4c (0.1028, 0.4660, 1/4), O2 8d (0.1961, 0.2014, 0.5531)
    (Horiuchi et al. 1987, ambient; the free parameters change by < 0.005 up to 25 GPa).
--abc a b c overrides the lattice; --ref-data FILE --ref-rep na nb nc takes a, b, c = box/rep from a perfect
LAMMPS cell (e.g. 1280atoms/V6.5669/bdg_2000K_100GPa.data, 4 4 4). The positions in that file are thermal, so
the Wyckoff parameters always come from the table above.

Geometry (crystal frame: x || a, y || b, z || c). For the plane (0kl), with k and l coprime,

    u  = [0 l -k] = (0, l b, -k c) / P_y,  P_y = sqrt((l b)^2 + (k c)^2)    in-plane period      (2)
    d  = 1 / sqrt((k/b)^2 + (l/c)^2)               (0kl) lattice-plane spacing                   (3)
    θ  = atan2(k/b, l/c)                           angle between n and c; misorientation 2θ      (4)
         (equivalently 180° - 2θ, because Pbnm has a 2-fold axis along a)

```
# Equilibrium grain-boundary sliding in a z-normal bicrystal: centre-of-mass motion of the two grain interiors.
# The relative displacement u = com(A) - com(B) diffuses with D_u = k_B T/(2 beta A) (two boundaries, friction
# coefficient beta per area A = Lx Ly); see tools/gb_slide.py. NVT equilibration, then NVE (no thermostat friction).
# Required -var: DATA MODEL TEMP NEQ NRUN SEED TIMEOUT ZA1 ZA2 ZB1 ZB2 ZB3 ZB4 (from tools/gb_grains.py)
# Optional -var: RX RY (replicate the cell in x and y: boundary area x RX*RY, for the size test; default 1 1)
# Output: slide.dat (step comA_x y z comB_x y z T PE, every 10 steps);
#         msd.dat (step msd_Mg msd_O, whole cell, COM-corrected, every 1000 steps) -> boundary diffusion delta*D_b
units           metal
boundary        p p p
atom_style      atomic
timestep        0.001
variable        RX index 1
variable        RY index 1
read_data       ${DATA}
replicate       ${RX} ${RY} 1
mass            1 24.305
mass            2 16.000
neighbor        1.0 bin
neigh_modify    every 1 check yes
pair_style      deepmd ${MODEL}
pair_coeff      * *
timer           timeout ${TIMEOUT} every 1000
thermo          1000
thermo_style    custom step temp press pe etotal pxz pyz cpuremain
region          RA block INF INF INF INF ${ZA1} ${ZA2}
region          RB1 block INF INF INF INF ${ZB1} ${ZB2}
region          RB2 block INF INF INF INF ${ZB3} ${ZB4}
region          RB union 2 RB1 RB2
group           A region RA
group           B region RB
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J MgOgbsl
#SBATCH --nodes 1
#SBATCH --ntasks 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 9
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:p100:1
#SBATCH --exclude=hpc-93-36
#SBATCH --partition gpu
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2GB
#SBATCH --time=06:00:00
#SBATCH --mail-user=rcohen@carnegiescience.edu

# Equilibrium GB sliding runs (tools/gb_slide.lammps), one task per line of gbtasks.txt (dir TEMP DATA).
# Run from the root holding gbtasks.txt and graph_c.pb: sbatch --array=1-N gb_slide_array.sh. TIMEOUT = 6 h - 300 s.

ulimit -s unlimited

ROOT=$PWD
read D TEMP DATA <<< "$(grep -v '^#' gbtasks.txt | sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p")"
mkdir -p $D; cd $D

# Pbnm general positions (x, y, z)
OPS = [(( 1,  1,  1), (0, 0, 0)), ((-1, -1,  1), (0, 0, .5)), (( 1, -1, -1), (.5, .5, 0)), ((-1,  1, -1), (.5, .5, .5)),
       ((-1, -1, -1), (0, 0, 0)), (( 1,  1, -1), (0, 0, .5)), ((-1,  1,  1), (.5, .5, 0)), (( 1, -1,  1), (.5, .5, .5))]

def pbnm_cell():
    """Fractional coordinates and types of the 20-atom Pbnm cell."""
    fr, ty = [], []
    for t, w in WYCK:
        orb = []
        for s, tr in OPS:
            p = (np.array(s) * w + tr) % 1.0
            if not any(np.linalg.norm((p - q + .5) % 1 - .5) < 1e-4 for q in orb):
                orb.append(p)
        fr += orb; ty += [t] * len(orb)
    fr, ty = np.array(fr), np.array(ty)
    assert np.bincount(ty)[1:].tolist() == [4, 4, 12], np.bincount(ty)
    return fr, ty

def geometry(abc, k, l):
def write(fn, pos, typ, box, v, title, comments):
    with open(fn, 'w') as f:
        f.write(f"{title}\n")
        for c in comments:
            f.write(f"# {c}\n")
        f.write(f"\n{len(typ)} atoms\n3 atom types\n\n")
        for k, ax in enumerate('xyz'):
            f.write(f"0 {box[k]:.6f} {ax}lo {ax}hi\n")
        f.write("\nMasses\n\n" + "".join(f"{t} {MASS[t]}  # {NAME[t]}\n" for t in (1, 2, 3)) + "\nAtoms # atomic\n\n")
        for i, (p, t) in enumerate(zip(pos, typ)):
            f.write(f"{i+1} {t} {p[0]:.6f} {p[1]:.6f} {p[2]:.6f}\n")
        if v is not None:
            f.write("\nVelocities\n\n")
            for i, vv in enumerate(v):
                f.write(f"{i+1} {vv[0]:.6f} {vv[1]:.6f} {vv[2]:.6f}\n")

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Locate the two boundaries of a z-normal bicrystal (LAMMPS data file) from the minima of the smoothed atom density
along z, and print the z ranges of the two grain interiors (margin W from each boundary) as LAMMPS -var arguments:
  -var ZA1 .. -var ZA2 .. -var ZB1 .. -var ZB2 .. -var ZB3 .. -var ZB4 ..
Grain A = [ZA1, ZA2]; grain B = [ZB1, ZB2] U [ZB3, ZB4] (the second block handles wrapping through z = 0).
usage: gb_grains.py DATA [--w 8]
"""
import argparse
import numpy as np

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument('data'); ap.add_argument('--w', type=float, default=8.0)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    L = open(a.data).read().split('\n')
    n = int([l for l in L if l.strip().endswith('atoms')][0].split()[0])
    zl = [l for l in L if 'zlo' in l][0].split(); z0, z1 = float(zl[0]), float(zl[1]); Lz = z1 - z0
    i = [k for k, l in enumerate(L) if l.startswith('Atoms')][0]
    z = (np.array([float(l.split()[4]) for l in L[i + 2:i + 2 + n]]) - z0) % Lz
    nb = 200
    h, e = np.histogram(z, bins=nb, range=(0, Lz))
    k = np.exp(-0.5 * (np.arange(-15, 16) * Lz / nb / 1.5) ** 2); k /= k.sum()     # 1.5 A Gaussian, periodic
    hs = np.real(np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(h) * np.fft.fft(np.r_[k[15:], np.zeros(nb - 31), k[:15]])))
    c = 0.5 * (e[1:] + e[:-1])
    b1 = c[np.argmin(hs)]
    far = np.abs(((c - b1 + Lz / 2) % Lz) - Lz / 2) > Lz / 4                         # the other minimum is ~Lz/2 away
    b2 = c[far][np.argmin(hs[far])]
    b1, b2 = sorted([b1, b2])
    za = (b1 + a.w, b2 - a.w); zb = (b2 + a.w, b1 + Lz - a.w)
    if zb[0] >= Lz:
13:    ap.add_argument('data'); ap.add_argument('--w', type=float, default=8.0)

## Jobs submitted

All runs use the Deng model at Cordier's four geotherm states (30 GPa/2000 K, 60/2300, 90/2500, 120/2800), plus Fei's 27 GPa/2200 K. The record is `LAMMPS/DengStates/README.md`.

| job | what | what it gives |
|---|---|---|
| 4612142 (10 tasks) | Constant-pressure (NPT) lattice runs: MgO (512 atoms) and bridgmanite (960 atoms) at all 5 states | a, b, c, volume and energy per atom at each state |
| 4612192 (3 tasks) | Bridgmanite (021), (013) and (011) tilt boundaries at 30 GPa: 32 shifted starting structures per plane, each energy-minimised | Lowest boundary energy per plane, compared with van Driel's 1.41 J/m² for (021) |
| 4612246 (5 tasks, starts after 4612142) | Boundary diffusion in the MgO Σ5 bicrystal: 50 ps NPT, then 1 ns at fixed volume, positions saved every 1 ps | Mg and O boundary diffusivity δD_b at each state, the input to the Cordier comparison |
| 4612253 (starts after 4612142) | MgO polycrystal, about 26,000 atoms in 8 grains, minimised then annealed for 300 ps at 60 GPa/2300 K | Relaxed boundaries for the grain-size model |

**Diffusion analysis tool:** `tools/gb_diff.py` computes diffusion as a function of distance from the boundary, with the sliding of the two grains removed, and from that δD_b.
- On synthetic data with a known answer it recovers δD_b to within 2 %.
- One design point: if sliding is removed with a smooth ramp across the boundary, δD_b comes out 60 % too high when the real sliding is a sharp step. So the default subtracts the displacement of the grain on each side.

**Risks:**
- I haven't tested a 26,000-atom cell with this model on the P100s, so memory may run out.
- Only one terminating atomic layer was used for the bridgmanite boundaries, while van Driel also varied it.
- At 120 GPa the Σ5 boundary may not move at all, as we saw at 140 GPa with the MgO-only model.

Records are updated: INPROGRESS, DONE, restart item 9. The results summary had OCTP still listed as an open item, so I marked it done.

## r-RESPA with DeePMD

**Why it fails now:** the DeePMD pair style declares it can't split its forces into inner, middle and outer distance ranges, and LAMMPS refuses r-RESPA on that basis. A single network can't be split by distance anyway.

**A route with no code changes:** LAMMPS can also assign whole pair styles to different r-RESPA levels, and that path skips this check (`src/respa.cpp`). So:
- **Inner level (small steps):** a cheap short-range potential F_s, such as a table or Buckingham pair potential fitted to DeePMD forces, with no Ewald sum.
- **Outer level (large steps):** DeePMD minus F_s, using `pair_style hybrid/scaled` with a −1 scale on a second copy of F_s.

```
pair_style hybrid/scaled 1.0 table linear 2000 1.0 deepmd graph_c.pb -1.0 table linear 2000
run_style  respa 2 3 hybrid 1 2 2
```

The physics stays DeePMD's; F_s only has to carry the fast vibrations.

**Expected gain:** only about 2–3×.
- MgO and bridgmanite vibrations are slow enough that 1 fs is already conservative. The outer step is limited to about 2–3 fs by resonance and by how well F_s tracks the fast modes.
- Total cost is about (DeePMD + n × cheap)/(outer step), and the inner evaluations are almost free.
- Recent machine-learned-potential versions of this trick (a small inner model with a large-model correction) report similar 2–4× speedups.

**The more involved alternative:** train a short-cutoff DeePMD model plus a residual long-range model and put them on separate levels. That means training two models, for about the same 2–4×.

**Why it doesn't change our strategy:** a factor of 2–3 doesn't touch the 10⁶–10¹² gap to seismic periods, so driving the system plus barrier-based rates remain the main route. It would help the long dislocation and boundary MD runs, such as the 9–12 h D1 and D1b jobs.

**Testing it** would take about half a day: fit F_s to existing DeePMD frames, then run a 4096-atom MgO energy-drift and speed test at 1 fs inner and 2, 3 and 4 fs outer. Should I go ahead?

### Claude (10-15 12:49)

Agreed, I've dropped r-RESPA. A bigger time step is free to try, so I've submitted a test of 1 to 5 fs (job 4620528). It starts automatically once the lattice runs (4612142) finish, and takes about 1–2 h per state.

**My guess (rough numbers):** 2–3 fs will be safe, and 5 fs will probably run stably but run slightly hot.
- **Fastest vibrations:**
  - MgO's highest optical mode is about 22 THz at 0 GPa and probably 30 THz or more at 120 GPa, a period of roughly 30 fs.
  - Bridgmanite's Si–O stretching modes are similar at high pressure.
- **Stability:** the integrator only blows up when ω·dt > 2, which here means dt above roughly 10 fs. So 5 fs (ω·dt ≈ 1) should be stable.
- **Accuracy at 5 fs:** the error grows roughly as (ω·dt)². I expect the effective temperature and pressure to shift by a few percent, plus some energy drift.

**The test:**
- **States:** MgO at 30 GPa/2000 K, MgO at 120 GPa/2800 K, and bridgmanite at 120 GPa/2800 K. All use the Deng model and start from the new lattice runs.
- **For each step of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 fs:**
  - 20 ps at constant energy, to measure energy drift;
  - 20 ps at constant temperature, to measure the shifts in temperature, potential energy and pressure against 1 fs.
- **Analysis:** `tools/dt_test.py DengStates/dt_test/*` writes one table per state.
- **Choosing the step:** I'll take the largest step that keeps drift under about 1 meV/atom/ps and the pressure shift under about 0.5 GPa. A 0.5 GPa shift is small next to the model's own errors against DFT.

Going from 1 to 3–5 fs would give the factor of 3–5 that r-RESPA promised, with nothing to fit or maintain. If 4–5 fs passes, I'll use it for the long dislocation and boundary runs.

Records are updated in the DengStates README, INPROGRESS, DONE and the restart file. None of the jobs submitted earlier today has started yet; I'll check their first outputs when they do.

### Claude (10-16 13:56)

I've written the new restart file, `ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-10-16.md`, and brought INPROGRESS and the DengStates README up to date. Checking the queue turned up several finished jobs and one problem.

**Finished and analysed:**
- **Lattice runs (4612142):** all 10 finished. MgO and bridgmanite a, b, c and volume at all five states are tabulated in the restart file (§3). For example, MgO is 4.089 Å at 30 GPa/2000 K and 3.786 Å at 120 GPa/2800 K.
- **Bridgmanite boundary energies at 30 GPa (4612192):** all three planes finished, but the energies are about twice van Driel's. The lowest values are 3.40 J/m² for (021), 3.36 for (013) and 2.36 for (011). For (021) that is about 2.4× van Driel's 1.41 J/m² at 25 GPa.
  - Leaving out the pressure–volume part (about 0.6 J/m²), it is still about 2×.
  - The most likely cause is that minimising straight from rigidly shifted cells gets stuck in high-energy structures. The energies across the 32 shifts spread from 2.4 to 4.5 J/m², which fits that.
  - Two other gaps: I only built one terminating atomic layer, and van Driel also varied which atoms were removed at the boundary.
  - Next: a short high-temperature anneal and quench of the best few shifts, plus a scan over terminating layers. I'm treating the current numbers as preliminary.

**Finished, not yet analysed:** the dislocation runs D1 (4593708–11) and D1b (4602367/8). D1b fit in the P100 memory.

**Still queued:**
- Σ5 boundary diffusion (4612246), now free to start;
- polycrystal anneal (4612253);
- time-step test (4620528);
- PBE check (4520046).

The restart file lists the priorities for the next session: analyse D1/D1b, check the first outputs of the new runs, fix the bridgmanite boundary-energy discrepancy, then the PBE comparison.
